speechtext:
As I always want to he eminently consistent I shall not pursue' that branch of the argument, but as suggested by my friend (Mr. Lancaster) I shall pursue some of the other branch lines. These three companies are substantially one and the same company, the Grand Trunk, the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company. The government is building the eastern division, and from day to day as time goes on we are more and more realizing the amount of money we are putting into that enterprise. The advantages are all in favour of the railway companies as contrasted with the position of the country. The Grand Trunk Pacific Company get all the good end and we get all the bad end ; they get all the easy part and we get all the difficult part, and therefore the government should safeguard the people to the extent of seeing that if we put our money into the building of this eastern division, and we are compelled to take it over at the end of fifty years, or if after it is built-and this is not a remote contingency-the Grand Trunk Pacific Company do not take it at all, but it is left on our hands, we should be able to obtain such branch lines as are feeders to it or as connect the cities of the south with it, upon reasonable terms. Now, in the Act of 1904 we have the provision which, as the Minister of Railways says, is copied in the amendment which he proposed the other day, 'that the government shall, if at the expiration of the said Mr. LENNOX.
lease if it shall determine to undertake the operation of the said eastern division, take over such branch line or lines as the company' may elect not to retain.' The position is this, that if in any event we operate the line at the end of the fifty-year period, we have not the right to take over the paying branches, but we are compelled, whether we want to do so or not, to take over the branches which the railway company do not want to retain, which will be the branches which are not paying. We have not an option, as under the amendment I propose, of taking them over. If we have an option, it is beneficial to this country, but if we are saddled with the necessity of taking them over, whether we want them or not, and are compelled to take over such branch lines as the company do not desire to retain our position is not only not improved in over what it was when this Bill came into the House some weeks ago, but we are in a vastly worse position. I protest against that condition of things. Let me call the minister's attention to something else. I was inclined to think that the minister had paid very little attention to the drafting of this amendment, not only because I did not find the proviso in ' Hansard ' or anywhere else or get any track of it until the minister mentioned it now, but because this section, as now worded, is practically senseless. Let me call the minister's attention to how it works out. It says :
At such value as may be agreed upon, or as may, in case of failure so to agree, be determined in the manner provided by paragraph 24 (2) of the said contract.
There is no contract in this Act that we are amending. Before that it says :
The government shall, if at the expiration of the said lease-
There is no lease mentioned in the statute we are dealing with. This is simply very slovenly-if the minister will allow me to say so-and unsuitable wording to accomplish any purpose. This is brought in without consideration from a statute which deals with a lease and with an agreement, but the statute we are dealing with refers to neither lease nor agreement, and, therefore, the amendment in that respect is not appropriately drawn. I will not take much time over that, because it can be easily amended. But, more than that, this provision is meaningless. If we turn to the statute that it is taken from-that is paragraph 24 of section 2 of the agreement -we find that that provides :
If, in any question arising under the provisions of sub-paragraph s (a), (c) and (e) of this paragraph, the parties shall fail to agree, the matter in difference shall be determined by 'arbitrators, to be appointed in the manner provided by paragraph forty-seven of this agreement:	provided, however, that, if a
board of railway commissioners shall be here-

after appointed under the authority of an Act of the Parliament of Canada, having powers substantially as proposed by Bill No. 21 of the present session of parliament, then such dispute shall be determined by such board, from whose decision herein either party shall have the right, without leave, to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.
Now, when we turn to paragraphs (a), (c) and (e) we find that paragraph (a) Is ' reserving to the government, in respect of its ownership, present and future, of the Intercolonial and any other line or lines of railway, running powers and haulage rights over the eastern division of the railway ; paragraph (c) is ' securing to the government in respect of its ownership, running powers and haulage rights over the western division,' and paragraph (e) is ' securing to the company running powers and haulage rights over the Intercolonial Railway or any portion thereof.' How can that have any application to the matter we are dealing with now? Evidently the minister or whoever drafted this did not turn to the sections and see how they would work out, and the result is that when we do trace them up we find that they become absolutely senseless. If the minister does not want to adopt the full measure of relief that I propose I regret it very much, but in any event, if he sincerely wants to have this workable, and I have no doubt he does, he should frame a provision somewhat on the lines on which I framed it, making it complete in its wording.

speechtext: I am afraid 1 shall have to make my remarks longer than I had intended. I thought the hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles! and every other member of this House understood the peculiarity of this charter. Here was a very vexed question beginning in 1903. The two

political parties disagreed as to the wisdom of the bargain made with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. We made a certain arrangement with the company wherein we were almost sure to lose- much more sure to lose if they did not make money than if they did. The probabilities of the company earning money and paying dividends had everything to do with whether the guarantees of this government as endorsed would fall upon them, that is whether we should be called upon to make good the money that the Grand Trunk Pacific would borrow on the strength of the guarantee. In 1906, when the Branch Lines Company was to be incorporated, 1 took the position in the Railway Committee and in this House that we ought not to create another entity with power to build branch lines, but that the building of the branch lines should be part and parcel of the Grand Trunk Pacific. My argument was-and, if I do say it myself, it was never answered-that, in case of a dispute as to division of freight between a company originating traffic and the trunk line which takes over that traffic and carries to its destination as to the division of the freight, the railway commissioners would probably, and very properly, give the lion's share to the originating company; therefore, if we guaranteed the liabilities of 'A' and then permitted him to carry on in the name of ' B ' a business more profitable than that which he carried on in his own name
Did the Grand Trunk Pacific represent ' B ' in that case?

The Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company is not the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. The case is as if the hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles) were to ask me to endorse his note and then ho were to carry on the profitable part of his business in his wife's name and yet, while allowing her to make the profits, would refuse to make her responsible for the obligation on which I had endorsed. It would be as though a man went to a bank for money and the bank were to say; If you get So and So to guarantee you, we will give you the money; then, having got the money, he divides his business into profitable and unprofitable parts, makes it impossible for the endorser to gain any of the profits and yet leaves him liable for an obligation which could not be redeemed because relating to the unprofitable part. In plain English, that is what we did when we incorporated the Branch Lines Company. Of course, we cannot go back on that. I am not suggesting that; but the hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles) asked me why it made a difference, and I am trying to tell him. I understand that my hon. friend from South Simcoe wants to try to stop this from going any further.

The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) does not understand me. There is no evidence that the capital to be put into the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines is in the slightest way identical or associated with the Grand Trunk Pacific. If he will show me any reason for believing that it is, one great doubt in my mind will be removed.

I do not think it makes any difference how they raise the money. These two are the same concern, the same people. Nobody believes anything else. The hon. gentleman himself (Mr. Knowles) will not say that they are different.
I think so.
A different crowd?
Before the lines are built and in operation, there may be different capitals invested altogether.

Well let us see who the men are in this Branch Lines Company. Here for instance, is Mr. Charles M. Hays. Everybody knows who Mr. Hays is-he is president of the Grand Trunk Pacific, and second vice-president and general manager of the Grand Trunk. Then there is Mr. Frank W. Morse, who is vice-president and general manager of the Grand Trunk Pacific. Then there is Mr. William Wainwright. Does not everybody know that he is one of the principal officers of the Grand Trunk and Grand Trunk Pacific? Another is Mr. W. H. Biggar, who, as we all know, was assistant solicitor of the Grand Trunk and who now occupies the position formerly held by Mr. John Bell as general solicitor of the Grand Trunk Railway system. And then there is Mr. D'Arcy Tate, assistant solicitor of the Grand Trunk Railway. Now those are the people who are incorporated in the name of the Branch Lines Company.

I would remind the hon. gentleman that the gentlemen who take out a charter are not necessarily those who will finance the charter. There is absolutely no reason to believe that because Mr. Wainwright, Mr. Biggar and their associates have taken out a charter, that therefore some of the investors' money is going to be in that railroad.

I do not say that the same people are going to lend the money to build the road, but these are the principal debtors whose liabilities the government of this country are going to guarantee, these are the people who can make us liable on these bonds that we guarantee, according to how they manage their affairs. The Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Branch Lines Company are one and the

same concern so far as relates to the running of that railway and the making or losing of money, and therefore the sticking the people of this country so to speak, on their bonds. Now some such amendment as proposed by my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) is necessary at this juncture. No one has said yet that there is anything wrong with it, every one has said that there is no objection to it. Theii it goes on to say :
If any such line of railway, so to be taken over, shall have received any grant or grants under the provisions of any Act of the Parliament of Canada, the amount of such grant or grants, without interest, shall be deducted from such value, and the difference only shall be payable by the government upon the taking over of the line.
Now why is not that only fair but necessary, in the interest of the country ? But now the minister proposes to withdraw his amendment on condition that the hon. member for South Simcoe withdraws his; in that case we will have neither. The proposition of the Minister of Railways that brought me to my feet, was that if he succeeded in getting my hon. friend from South Simcoe to drop his amendment, he. the minister, would drop the amendment to the amendment, and in that case we would have neither the one nor the other. I appeal to the Minister of Railways if that provision should not be either in this amendment to the amendment, or in the original amendment of my hon. friend from South Simcoe. I say again that it is absolutely necessary if we are not going to let the Grand Trunk, and the Grand Trunk Pacific, and the Grand Trunk Branch Lines, and any other concern that the Grand Trunk chooses to put before this country as a company that is going to be affiliated with it-I say if we are not going to let them do anything they please, if we are not going to hand over to them the sole control of everything in sight, and the right to tax the people to this extent, then we must put some such amendment as this in the Bill. Then it says :
Provided, however, that nothing in this Act contained shall authorize the government to take over the said lines of railway or any of them without the consent of parliament, previously obtained, to the exercise of such right of taking over as aforesaid.
Now surely we have got to have some such provision. If the Minister of Railways will draw a section that protects the people, though it uses different language from this. I will support it. But we must have something of that kind somewhere in this Bill. When we passed this charter in 1906, I, over and over again, to the extent of making myself an annoyance perhaps to some gentlemen in the Railway Commission, insisted on a clause that nothing we did for that Branch Lines Company should interfere with any of the rights of the people in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific. That did not carry. Why ? Because the Grand Trunk Pacific would not have it, and the government would not force the Grand Trunk Pacific to take it. It was argued that we were incorporating a different company, under a different name, which would be capitalized perhaps by uifferent people, and therefore, although they were- going to become affiliated with the Grand Trunk Pacific, we should not force them to relieve us from liability on the bonds of the Grand Trunk Pacific. I proposed in the Railway Commission, and I think again in the House, that there should be a clause in the Grand Trunk Branch Lines Company charter that nothing therein contained should impair or take away the right of the people in regard to the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, or should put them in the same position as if the Grand Trunk Pacific itself had built these branch lines under the original charter. and that was voted down by this House. Everybody in this country knows that the Grand Trunk Pacific and the Grand Trunk Branch Lines Company are one and the same concern, and are working for the benefit of the Grand Trunk Railway. Therefore when we proposed in 1906 that nothing in this Act which is now being amended should take away any of the rights that we had already, and that everything we did for that company should have the same effect, as regards these branch lines when they were built, as if they had been built by the Grand Trunk Pacific themselves, when we could not get that, when the government voted that dowm, the present Minister of Justice who took charge of the measure instead of the then Minister of Railways, put in that qualified section which is now being amended, that it should not affect our rights in some regards only. Now the hon. member for West Assiniboia (Mr. Knowles) must recognize that his own side of this question was represented in this House^ in 1906 by the present Minister of Justice, who drafted and put in a clause dealing wdth the principle of the matter, but not to the full extent it ought to be dealt with, that is to say. that the Branch Lines Company was connected w'ith the Grand Trunk Pacific, and vou will find in the original Act of the Branch Lines Company a clause saying that it should not affect the right of the country ns against the Grand Trunk Pacific Company in some respects, and in those respects only. But my point is that this government did undertake to say that the one had something to do with the other, that thev should be dealt with in some respects as if they were one and the' same
If my hon. friend wants to tell us that the Grand Trunk Branch Lines Company and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company are entirely different matters and should

not be mixed up the best answer I can give him is the section of the Act of 1906 which was drawn by the Minister of Justice and -which says to the contrary. I and another hon. gentleman made the contention in the Railway Committee that there should be full protection to the people but we succeeded in getting only a compromise and not the full measure of protection that I thought ought to be enunciated in the Act. I want to say to my hon. friend that the Minister of Justice declared in this section the very opposite to what my hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals tells us should be adopted when he put this clause into the Act in lieu of the one which I was moving which was more general in its terms and which was designed to protect the people entirely and not in the limited -way that this does. Section 32 of the Act to incorporate the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company, passed in 1906, provides that:
,,Tllie Provlslons of paragraphs 39, 12, 13 and 11 ot the agreement which forms the .schedule to chapter 71 of the statutes of 1903, and so much of paragraph 15 of the said agreement as provides that traffic shall not (be diverted to ports outside of Canada, shall apply to the company in the same manner and to the same extent as if the lines of railway hereby authorized .had been constructed by the Grand 1 rumk Pacific Railway Company.
Surely, iu view of that, my hon. friend will not say that there is nothing at all in the contention that one company is affiliated with the other and that we should not mix them up in legislation. Surely, in view of the section passed by this parliament, drawn by the Minister of Justice and offered to parliament in lieu of the full protection that I was contending for iu the interests of the people iu every respect, my hon friend will apologize to the House and recognize that he was entirely wrong in saying that they were two companies and that they were not connected one with the other. The Minister of Justice knew that in these matters that are mentioned here there must l)e some protection in regard to the people's rights, in regard to the guarantees which they gave and the benefits they expected to receive from the incorporation and development of this company or scheme known as the National Transcontinental Railway and the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company this ocean to ocean line. The Minister of Justice recognized, although he was. as I thought and still think, not doing what he ought to have done to protect the people m regard to the guarantees and the great liabilities which they were assuming in assisting the Grand Trunk Pacific to construe! this line, that in that matter the statute should lie amended and he put in the clause which I have just quoted and which distinctly says that these paragraphs shall apply in the same manner aud to the same extent as if the lines of railway hereby

authorized had been constructed by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. I am afraid that the Minister of Railways and Canals sometimes forgets that all we are doing by this Branch Lines Railway Company could have been done by the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company itself. I always was opposed to giving the Branch Lines Company these rights as it looked to me like an attempt to give another company, under an entirely different name, but with the same people behind it, the right to acquire all the benefits that the branch lines will give them because this will be the paying part of the railway and at the same time not make provision to assist the parent company which is our debtor and which is the debtor of the capitalists who have taken the bonds guaranteed by the country. My hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) proposes here an amendment that if any of these branch lines are taken over by the government the government shall be able to select the lines they want. As it is now the government have to take the lines that the Grand Trunk do not want, only such lines as the Grand Trunk choose! to use an ordinary expression, to dump upon the people of the country. Such lines as they have found do not pay them very well they can force the people to take. Surely we can get over that. Let us have a little judgment. The right hon. gentleman who leads the House knows the absolute freedom from entangling and suspicious connections which that great parliamentarian, Mr. Gladstone, always insisted upon. It was one of the very bright spots in his brilliant career that he insisted upon all the members of his government keeping free not only from business connections which would in any way embarrass the actions of the government, but all connections which would at all bring suspicion upon the high position which he was determined should be occupied by himself and his ministers. Then I call the attention of the right hon. gentleman to the case of the Rt. Hon. W. H. Smith-to one circumstance in his life which is related in a letter he wrote to the president or other high official of the Bank of England at a time when it was in an embarrassed position. He said no. He wrote back :	* I will advance to the bank

I will certainly. As I said, shortly after my return from Europe, I received a letter from Mr. Williams, which was read by the hon. member for North Toronto, and which therefore I will not read again, calling my attention to what he deemed to he an injustice committed towards himself by the Minister of Agriculture, in this, that he had been an applicant for a subsidy voted by parliament for the establishment of a cold storage, that his application had been denied, and that the same subsidy had been given to a company in which the Minister of Militia had interested himself. He did not put tlie latter fact to me in the words I have Indicated, on the contrary, lie stated in so many words that the subsidy had been given to a company in which the Minister of Militia had a prominent interest-I forget the exact words at the present time ; but I know my hon. friend will agree with me that that was the sense of the letter which was addressed to me. It was my duty therefore under the circumstances to give some attention to the matter, and I did it all the more readily because I understood that Mr. Williams was a very respectable citizen of the city of St. John, and also a prominent Liberal. It is of no particular interest to the House to remind it that the policy which had been introduced by the Minister of Agriculture of bonusing plants for cold storage in different parts of the country, had been received with great favour by both sides of this House. The Minister of Agriculture had also come to the conclusion that it would be in the public interest that such a plant should be established in the city of St. John, and I

One was by Mr. Williams himself, one was by Mr. Macoun, who is the son-in-law of the Minister of Militia, and Defence, and who acted in behalf of the company of which it is no use to speak at any length at this moment. Both these applications had the support of friends. Mr. Macoun's application was supported by the Minister of Militia, who was a colleague of the Minister of Agriculture. The application of Mr. Williams was supported by my then colleague, the Minister of Railways and Canals of that day, the present member for Westmoreland (Mr. Emmerson). As is natural under such circumstances the Minister of Militia and the Minister of Railways of that day favoured, as best they could, the interests of their respective applicants. Under such circumstances X put it to my hon. friend from North Toronto. (Mr. Foster), I put it to any man in this House : What should be the attitude of the Minister of Agriculture ? Here were two parties, both respectable, both represented to be able to carry out this contract, both represented to be able to perform the duties attached to it and both having the support behind them of their respective friends. What was the
___Minister of Agriculture to do ? If mv hon.
friend from North Toronto had been Minister of Agriculture, what would he have done ? What could he have done ? In what manner could he have disposed of the question ? The Minister of Agriculture thought, and thought very properly, that under such circumstances he would give the subsidy to the party who, in his opinion, could show that he was the more deserving, the better equipped and the more likely to carry out the intent of the Act ; that is to say, to promote the commercial policy which was involved in the voting of the subsidy by parliament. Mr. Macoun, in behalf of the company which he represented, filed his plan and specification, showed to the ministers, in black and white by an actual document deposited in his hands, how lie was prepared to earn the subsidy voted by parliament, what he proposed to do, the buildings, the equipment and the plant which he proposed to erect. The Minister of Agriculture could not have done otherwise than to ask Mr. Williams to file his plans and specifications so that he might judge between the two applications which had the better equipment and to which the subsidy should go in order best to accomplish the object parliament had in view in voting it. Mr. Williams is a political friend of mine though not a personal friend, and when I looked into the papers I wrote him my opinion very plainly. If my memory serves me right the Department of Agriculture asked Mr. Williams not once but on two or three occasions to file his plans and specifications. Last fall when I was appealed to I looked into the matter with some care and consideration-I do not say I looked into it minutely so as to become acquainted with all the details, but I looked into it sufficiently to satisfy myself as to the salient points and these salient points I have stated to the House and upon them the Minister of Agriculture gave his decision.

It matters not what happened before, but the contract was awarded to the New Brunswick Cold Storage Company and we have the word of the Minister of Militia, which has not been contradicted, that he has no interest whatever either directly or indirectly in that company. If the Minister of Militia had been connected with the New Brunswick Cold Storage Company, then I would understand the lecture which has been given us by the member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) as to the character which ought to prevail in public life in this country. I have no exception to take to the statements of the hon. member on this point, I agree with him entirely. But whilst it is very true that the code of ethics in Great Britain is what he has stated it to be, that no public man should be interested at all in any company or association which may have anything to do, directly or indirectly, with the government, is. he prepared to say that that has been

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: the code of ethics in this country? Is he prepared to say that the same code of ethics which has prevailed in England and which I agree with him ought to prevail in this country, has been the code here ? Surely he ' knows the history of this country too well not to know that this has not been the code in this country. I do not care to quote examples and would not quote them, but for the fact that one has been quoted to-day, the case of Hon. Thomas White, who was owner of the Montreal * Gazette.' Mr. White was one of the most honourable men who ever sat in this House, but he was connected with the Montreal ' Gazette ' which had a large printing contract with the government of that day. Some exception was taken to this, and the answer was that the law of the country allowed it, and that (he seat of the member could not be imperilled, that a member of the government or of parliament could be associated in a company which had dealings with the government. That was the code of ethics twenty years ago. The hon. member for Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) says that we should have another code of ethics, that we should not be satisfied and that we should make it the rule that no member of parliament and especially of the government should be connected with auy association or company that may have any dealings with the government. I subscribe altogether to this * doctrine. It Is new in the political life in this country, but it is not too late to accept it. I am prepared to accept it in its entirety. My hon. friend lias quoted Sir Henry Lennox, Mr. Chamberlain and other men in Great Britain who, in order to be absolutely above reproach, have taken some action on which the hon. member has commented favourably. Mr. Chamberlain stated in the House on a charge brought against him that he had severed his connection with all the companies with which he had been associated, and which had contracts with the government. How is it that my hon. friend did not give the credit to the Minister of Militia of having done exactly the same thing in this matter. The Minister of Militia followed the example of Mr. Chamberlain. The minister stated so himself in the speech he delivered yesterday, saying that when he found the Minister* of Agriculture had introduced a Bill which was to provide for large subsidies he severed his connection absolutely with this organization.	,

The principle seems , to be that a man may go ahead and steal; if it is not discovered he keeps the money and if it is discovered he makes restitution and there is no punishment.

When irregularities occur the inspector suspends the officer and the commissioner approves of his suspension and the inspector then makes a thorough examination of the books and sends in "a final report. If the defalcation is made good the inspector reports that also and an order in council is passed dispensing with the services of the defaulting officer.

I can understand that a case may arise where an officer had been carelessi and the defalcation small and where there never had been any criminal intent ; I can understand that in such a case no proceedings should be taken when restitution is made. But here is a case where a man was several thousand dollars behind at a small outport and one hardly believe there was not criminal intent. Did the Minister conclude there was no criminal intent in this case ?

I think it was a bad case, and when the information came to me, as it only came through the remarks of the member for Brantford, we at once instructed Inspector Busby to go thoroughly into it, and the case was handed over to the Department of Justice.
Ij. BORDEN. Is the man under arrest ?
Inspector Busby telegraphed the otlier day that the man was arrested and pleaded guilty and will be sentenced on June 8.
Ij. BORDEN. Is there any security for the $5,800 ?

That has been paid.
Mr. FOWLER, Tell us about the Gardiner case at Fort McLeod.
That was for a small amount and restitution was made. That was dealt with by the guarantee company.
And there was no prosecution ?
No, they did not prosecute.

If that is not compounding a felony it comes perilously near it. According to the minister's statement, if the man makes restitution, which of course is no punishment, he is not prosecuted for his dishonesty and crime against the country. The people will believe that
the government are encouraging crime by not punishing these men.
I understood the leader of the opposition to say that there might be exceptional cases.
Ij. BORDEN. I said where there was no criminal intent.

It is very hard to tell about the criminal intent. The rule of the department has been that where there has been tampering with the money we have not been able to overlook it. If a man is overcome with liquor once or twice we stand that, or we stand carelessness, but where there is direct tampering with the funds, we have never hesitated to dismiss the person.
But you do not prosecute.
Is it to be understood that in every case there should be a criminal prosecution ?
Where there is criminal intent.
But where there is doubt about it and they say they have a very small salary and intend to pay it back-

It seems to me we have arrived at a most dangerous period in the history of our political life. A man may be caught stealing a loaf of bread to keep his family from starving and he is sent to jail, but a man can steal public money in connection with the civil service and we say : That is all right, pay it back at your leisure. It seems to me it is no excuse to say this has been going on for some time. We know it has been going on in the department of Customs to a very large extent. In the case brought up by the hon. member for Brantford, complaints had been made, an investigation was held and the man was censured. I understand he has not made restitution.
Yet all that was done in that case was the removal of the man for the time being from office. The information we have been able to drag from the Minister of Customs on these matters is very meagre. We need a new Civil Service Act, one that will place civil servants in this respect in the same position as all other classes of the community. Other institutions require their trusted officers to give security, either through a guarantee company or through friends ; but in some cases, in the civil service, a man guilty of defalcation is not even dismissed. We have had the promise of a new Civil Service Act ; but I do not know what advantage we can expect from it so long as there is only one class of the com-

munity who can take advantage of it. If a young man has not a pull, no matter what his ability is, there is no object in his passing the civil service examination. The time has come for removing the civil service from the political arena and awarding positions in it according to merit. So long as \ve permit the machine to recommend those appointed to positions in the service, we shall have the state of affairs that now exists. We have this year the enormous increase of $80,000 for extra work in the Customs Department. Last year the increase was $50,000 and the minister gave a long explanation of why that was required; but this evening he has chosen to take a different course, and he seems to think we should vote it off-hand without any explanation whatever. Now that it is half-past one, it seems to me that it is unwise to prolong this discussion, to hold up this House any longer. The opposition are not responsible for obstruction ; we would not be doing our duty to our constituencies and the country under existing circumstances if we did not do as we are doing. We have said to the government, bring down your important measures first ; bring down your Election Bill, which we have been alarmed about since this House met, which was promised in the Speech from the Throne, and which, if the government had not been afraid, would have been Drought down in the first two or three weeks of the session, but which they are trying to force through in the dying hours of the session.

It has been contended by many that the Minister of Customs has not been criticised by the opposition as much as would be for the good of the country. Everybody believes Mr. BARR.
he could not be anything but honest. I have no doubt if his officers were as honest as they should be the work would go on all right. But when you see $80,000 instead of $50,000 last year, for over-work, we know it is utterly impossible for the Minister of Customs, or any other minister, to supervise it and see that it is properly managed. And where there should be the protection of the Civil Service Act, we find that in many cases it is simply set aside. This looseness of administration is intended to allow the appointment of men unfit to fill these positions but who are recommended by the partisan supporters of the government. It is no wonder that we have so many defects in the Customs administration. There is no reason for this large amount spent in over-time
They do not allow us overtime when we work extra hours.

We are servants of the people and are expected to do anv kind of work at ail hours. Many of us who have seen the customs offiers at work know that it is impossible for the minister to know whether they are earning their money or not.

If we did so we should make more progress. We (have not accomplished much to-night and the minister knows we are not likely to accomplish much. I refer to the defalcation at Huntingdon. I say it is a very serious matter that such a defalcation should take place just a few months after our inspector had made this examination and reported all correct. When the information came to us from outside-I do not know whether from Mr. Kennedy or not- the officer was immediately told to go back to Huntingdon to investigate the report that there had been a defalcation.

That had happened after his previous visit or before?
Mi-. PATERSON. I think it happened before.
He ought to have found it the first time.

Certainly he should. It is impossible for myself or the commissioner or the deputy commissioner to know what is going on in such places as Huntingdon if our inspectors cannot be trusted to make correct reports. The inspector was an officer of thirty years' standing and had given faithful service. It may have been that the length of his service had detracted from his efficiency. He might have been superannuated before, and on the discovery of his error I thought I would not have him dismissed, but recommended that he should be superannuated. I had not the slightest idea, nor had our officers, that when the man went the second time, and especially after the rebuke that was given him, he would have failed to do the work thoroughly. I have given the minister all the statements that have come to me about this. Mr. B'OSTER. I do not think that any department should denude itself of the right to follow and punish a defaulter. It is responsible and the country will hold it accountable.

I do not think we should be too hard upon the Minister of Customs. The Minister of Customs has in all cases dismissed the party who defaulted. In some other departments in place of dismissing the defaulter they have promoted him and increased his salary. I have dismissed men from the service in whose behalf there have been pleas made by wives and sisters because I felt that as the administrator of a public department these things get out and have a bad influence upon the service. When this question came up it looked to me to be a very serious thing and I wanted to ascertain what the course of the department had been in the past. I made inquiries and my officers told me that they were not aware that there had been any prosecutions entered, although they were aware that there had been defalcations which had not been made good.

Of course these cases are all open and can be put into court at any time. I may say to the House that many of the men I had to dismiss had my sympathy and it takes all there is in me to be' impelled by a sense of duty to dismiss some of them. If there is any one who is interested in having the department right it is the minister. Whv, bless me. what is it after all. There is a salary attached to the portfolio, but what is that to a man who has a Proper public spirit. Is not the best of all that when a man is administering an office, that after he leaves it the people can say : Well, he did not know everything but he tried to do what was right. That is about ail the compensation there is for a public man.

I do not know it would be possible to advise the minister as to any rule to prosecute or not to prosecute in every case. It must be left to the head of the department who is responsible to parliament for his action. The method of inspection however might be discussed. I do not know what your method of inspection is, but Mr. Fyshe who had a great deal of banking experience seems to think that the method of inspection is not very perfect He commented upon the fact that you do not take precautions to keep secret the time at which your inspector would visit a particular collector. count of gale raging. The wharf at that place is almost impossible to make in rough weather, and our time-table provides that in such bad weather the boat would mot stop.

Mr. Speaker, before the orders of the day are called, I desire to rise to a question of privilege. On May 29 the Minister of Militia revised a statement made previously and published upon the ' Hansard.' His final statement, which I hope is correct as it appears, reads in this way :
I would like this House to consider whether at its worst it is to be compared for one moment with the position of a man who succeeds in placing himself in a position of trust in a company and then succeeds in placing himself in another position connected with another company, and then engages in the delightful occupation of buying lands for the company of which he was manager, and accepting a commission and putting it in his pocket in that connection-
I desire to say that the lands in question were not bought for the Union Trust Company, of which I was manager, they were not paid for by the moneys of the Union Trust Company ; not one dollar of commission was ever taken by me for lands purchased by me or by any one else for the Union Trust Company. The statement made by the hon. gentleman is entirely and absolutely untrue, and I ask him to retract it.

I did not name any particular company. I gave my authority the other day for the statement I made but, Mr. Speaker, since the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) states that the statement I made was not correct and that he did not do what I thought he had done and said he had done, I am the last man in the world to wish to misrepresent an hon. member, I am not in the habit of doing that, and I cheerfully withdraw the statement on the affirmation made by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) that what I stated was not true.

House in committee on Bill (No. 151) respecting the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company.-Mr. Crawford.
On section 1. (on the amendment to the amendment being read),

It seems to me that proposed amendment makes it very much
worse than it was, because it absolutely compels the government to take over such lines as the company desire to part with. The government without any such legislation, have the right to expropriate and to take over what lines they require, but that amendment absolutely compels the government to take over any lines the company desires to give up, no matter how unprofitable they may be or whether it would be unwise to operate them or not.

I certainly must object to this provision. It is in effect that parties coming here for a private Bill are granted a condition by this parliament compelling the government to take over the line of railway. I never heard of anything of the kind in a private Bill before. It is true that this is in reference to branch lines connected with the Transcontinental Railway, but here we have a private charter applied for by a company for the purpose of constructing a line and by this Bill we say to the company : You shall have the option at the end of a certnin period, when the government take possession of the Grand Trunk Pacific section of the National Transcontinental Railway, of taking over these lines. It is compulsory on the government to take over these lines.

So far as the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company is concerned, I think they will be only too glad if all the amendments are dropped. I think it was a great mistake to introduce amendments to the Bill at this time. This whole thing was fought out two years ago; it was fought out in committee and in this House. For months the Bill was held up and again in committee this year, and I do not see why amendments should be introduced at this time. It seems to me that the whole thing is a matter of obstruction and hold up. We have been renewing charters to railway companies right along here, session after session ; and, this session, I suppose some fifty charters have been renewed and the time extended, and not one company in the whole lot has been held up for a minute except the Grand Trunk Pacific.
Much better to have both withdrawn than to pass this one.

The only reason why the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) moved the amendment to the amendment, was that he thought the amendment was so unjust to the company, and that the amendment to the amendment would be an improvement. But as hon. members will recollect, he thought it better to have both amendments withdrawn. It seems to be that objection can be taken to both on the ground of justice. According to the amendment the government

could take over just what branches they liked, picking out the paying lines and leaving the others ; and, according to the amendment to the amendment, the company would have the choice of lines to he taken over by the government. It seems to me that, in the interest of justice, both should be withdrawn.

I suppose that the object of the hon. member for South Sim-coe (Mr. Lennox) was to make it possible for the government, in case it should operate the eastern division as a national enterprise, to control not only the main line but the feeders for that line. It does not require a great knowledge of railway operation to understand that that is an essential thing. The hon. member for South Simcoe was not inspired with any desire to hold up or obstruct this Bill; his wish, as I understand it, was to preserve what may be very important interests of the country in the future. It would be rather an anomalous condition to have the government operating the main line of the eastern division while all the feeders which bring business to that line were under the ownership and control of a private company. Of course an Act might be passed in the future to expropriate these branch lines, but it might not be very just to bring about that condition in future without notice in advance that it is, or might be the policy of the country. Whatever might be the merits or demerits of the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Simcoe, it seems to have a great deal to commend it-although it might properly be amended in the respect referred to by the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugs-ley). So far as the amendment to the amendment proposed by the Minister of Railways is concerned, there cannot J>e two opinions in the House as to that. To have the government operate the main line of the eastern division subject to having imposed upon it such feeders as had proved unprofitable, and were not desired to be retained by the Branch Lines Company, would be an entirely unheard of proposition, if the interests of the country are to be considered at all in the matter. The contract itself-the contract between the government and the Grand Trunk Pacific- looks to the possibility of the eastern division being operated, at some time or other, as a national enterprise. It is quite within the order of things that this should take place at the expiration of fifty years if I recollect the time correctly. We must look forward to that as a possibility, but must look forward also to the providing of feeders for that line, branch lines which the country will have the right to acquire. And, while it is not an immediate consideration, it is none the less a serious consideration Mr. PUGSLET.
as to what the rights of the country in that regard shall be. One would suppose that the interests of this Branch Lines Company might be properly preserved and full justice done to them consistently with the proposition that the country should at some future time operate not only the main line but the branches as well. It certainly would be a very incongruous condition, so far as that railway is concerned, if any other re suit should obtain in future.

Has the hon. Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) any information as to the intention of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company with regard to the branch line from Chipman to St. John ? During the recent election, in New Brunswick, Mr. Hays and Mr. Morse, of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company, went over the property of the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company, and the Minister of Public Works, if I remember correctly, intimated in more than one public speech that he expected to be able to announce in a short time the completion of arrangements for the purchase by the Grand Trunk Pacific of the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company for the use of the transcontinental line. I may say also that the hon. member for Carleton, N.B. (Mr. Carvell), in the course of the campaign, went so far as to state that announcement would be made of the close of the deal within a week from the date of his speech. I would like to know from the Minister of Public Works what position this matter is in. I observe a despatch in the Montreal ' Gazette ' of to-day stating that the Grand Trunk Pacific had no intention whatever of using the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company in connection with the transcontinental line.

I can only say that I have been informed upon several occasions by the principal officials of the Grand Trunk Pacific that they thought that the railway from Chipman to Norton, and thence either by a separate line, or by the Intercolonial, to St. John, would afford a very satisfactory means of reaching the harbour of St. John. They have stated to me more than once that they recognized the importance of getting a direct connection from the main line to St. John.
Does it run near Chip-man ?

It passes through Chip-man, and from the main line through St. John by way of Chipman is only 78 miles, and I think probably it is the shortest route they could take to St. John. They have suggested that they might branch off from the Chipman line a short distance from Norton and have a separate line to St. John, instead of using the Intercolonial. I know

also that they have been very much interested in the question of terminal facilities at the port of St. John and have considered the question of utilizing Courtenay Bay for their terminals. I think I was quite justified in making the statements I did in the past, because X had very positive assurance from the officials of the Grand Trunk Pacific that they were favourable to making this connection with St. John. X was also given the assurance that their determination would largely rest with the Minister of Railways, and not only had statements been made to myself, but there was the positive statement made in a public way by the then Minister of Railways (Mr. Emmerson), that he would favour the making of that connection with St. John. As to whether or not the Grand Trunk Pacific has changed its views with regard to the matter, I am not in a position to say. I think that my hon. friend (Mr. Crocket) must not take too seriously statements which he sees in the newspapers, particularly if they appear in telegraphic despatches from the province of New Brunswick. I understand my hon. friend to say that he saw this statement in a despatch published in the Montreal ' Gazette '. I am inclined to think that the sources of inspiration of the Montreal ' Gazette ' in the province of New Brunswick would be of a very partisan nature, and that, perhaps, statements might be made without most careful examination to see whether they rested upon a good foundation.

I understand that the minister (Mr. Pugsley) is yet quite hopeful that the Grand Trunk Pacific will take over the New Brunswick Coal and Railway Company for the purpose of connecting that line with the city of St. John ?

I may say that, since the change of government in the province of New Brunswick, I do not know that the provincial government would desire to part with the road. I have no intimation to that effect, and, of course, there must be a seller as well as a buyer.
Shall the amendment to the amendment be adopted ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
The Minister of Railways has given the policy of the government in this matter, and has said that he will not press the amendment to the amendment. He stated also, however, that he could not agree to the amendment of the hon. member for Simcoe either. I move, therefore, that the amendment to the amendment be withdrawn.
. Motion agreed to and amendment to the amendment withdrawn.
The question is now upon the amendment of the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox).
Does not the Prime Minister think that some provision should be made with reference to these branch lines having regard to the possibility of operation by the country ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I am sorry to say to my hon. friend that I do not agree with him. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals (Mr. Graham) has given his best attention to this subject and i find that he is of opinion that there is no necessity for such an amendment. The matter has been debated again and again and it seems to me that the amendment is rather meaningless because the power of the government to expropriate is always there.
The government has no power to expropriate without legislation.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is provided that nothing can be done except with the consent of parliament.

But this amendment sets out the conditions under which they may take these lines over. For instance, it is provided that any subsidy may be deducted and then the value is ascertained by arbitration. If the government decided to take them over without any provision except that of expropriation I assume that the company would be likely to set up the claim that on account of the enhanced value of the railway by virtue of the government subsidies which it had got they would be entitled to receive an additional compensation, whereas if this amendment passed they could not receive the amount of the subsidies, but they, on the contrary would be deducted.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER-No. The Bill reads that:
Provided, however, that nothing in this Act contained shall authorize the government to take over the said lines of railway or any of them without the consent of parliament previously obtained, to the exercise of such right of taking over as aforesaid.
If that right is to be exercised with the consent of parliament, which goes without saying, it is difficult to see what the object of this amendment is. However, it has been debated a great many times.
What is meant by ' aforesaid ' ? The aforesaid portion of the clause says that the amount of the subsidy the government has given to this company shall be deducted.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Do you think that fifty years from to-day parliament will * not' be at liberty to make any provision they

see fit ? At any rate, my hon. colleague the Minister of Railways and Canals has come to the conclusion that there is no necessity for the amendment.

I do not think there is a very great deal in that consideration. It would be necessary to obtain the consent of parliament whether that provision is inserted or not because parliament must make the necessary appropriation for the payment of the amount of the award. Mr. Gladstone, in 1849, I think it was, passed a statute in Great Britain which provided for the taking over of all the English railways and which still remains upon the statute-book as notice to every railway in the country that the government may take it over upon making the necessary parliamentary appropriation. The determination of the value was provided for in the statute, everything was done that was necessary except the parliamentary appropriation for the purpose and every railway in Great Britain to-day is under notice of that kind. The object of my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) was to have a provision in the charter of the company giving them notice that this might be done in a certain event and at a future period. It was, of course, necessary for him to provide, so that his amendment should be in order, that the right should not be exercised except with the consent of parliament. Parliament would require to make the necessary appropriation.
Amendment (Mr. Lennox) negatived.
On section 1. Extension of time for construction, commencement within two years after the passing of this Act and completion within five years.

How will this operate in connection with the original Bill ? The original Bill provided that the Transcontinental Railway was to be completed by 1911. Now we extend the time two years to commence these branch lines and then we give five years to finish them. That would make it 1913 at any rate, if not longer. We are giving power to extend the time for completing the branch lines two years beyond the time in which the Act provides the whole railway should be completed. I fancy that the government cannot expect that the railway will be completed within the time limit, or otherwise they would not be overriding their own Act in giving an extension of time to the subsidiary company for the commencement and completion of these branch lines after the time has expired for the completion of the whole line.

There can be no connection between the extension of time given in this charter and the provision which is contained in the original agreement with the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company. The fact that the branch lines com-Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
pany's time is extended cannot in any way affect and has no relation whatever to the provision as to the time of construction contained in the original agreement.

That is rather a strange kind of logic in view of the addresses which have been made in regard to this question. Hon. gentlemen opposite have always spoken of the system as a whole, of a completed line, and they have contended as well that it was necessary that not only the main line should be completed but that the branch lines should be built at the same time so that they might handle the produce of the west as well as goods being shipped from the east to the west and so that the system might be placed in connection with the great cities of the country, such as Montreal and Toronto. When it answers the purpose of these hon. gentlemen to speak of this system as a whole and of the advantage that would accrue to the country for having this great and important system finish in a few years they include the branch lines with the Grand Trunk Pacific, but when it answers their purpose and when there appears to be an incongruity between the powers which are given to this branch lines company and those which are contained in the original Bill, then it is contended that there is no connection between them. That is not the kind of argument that they addressed to this House before, and it does seem to me that it would be important to have certain of these branch lines at least finished at the time that the main line is put in operation. If it is to be in operation by 1911 and if these branch lines are necessary to connect the system with such cities as Montreal and Toronto and places like these it would seem to me to be desirable that the branch lines should be completed at the same time that the main line is put in operation, whereas, under this Bill it is not likely to be done.
What are the two branches that are named in the Act of 1906?
There is a great number of them named.
I thought there were just two.
No, there are ten or twelve.

As far as the branch lines are concerned the company are just as anxious as they can be to build them. They intend to go on with the construction of them as soon as the material and men can be got. Some of them are finally located now and are awaiting the approval of the department. Some of them will probably be started this season. There is no question as to the anxiety of the company to build new branch lines.

In reference to what the hon. gentleman (Mr. Crawford) has just said, there has been some considerable feeling throughout many parts of the Northwest owing to the failure of this branch lines company to commence the building of any of the branch lines which are included in this charter. The feeling is so great on this matter that petitions have been sent to the government asking them to refuse an extension of the charter. It is true this is a separate company from the Grand Trunk Pacific but, the two are undoubtedly very closely connected and the government in turn is very closely connected with the Grand Trunk Pacific Company. There is therefore reason in the request made from the Northwest that the government shall bring pressure to bear upon this company to commence the construction of these lines at the earliest possible moment. Early in the session I brought to the attention of the government the fact that the directors of the Grand Trunk Pacific Company had promised that they would soon commence the construction of the Regina York-ton branch and have it in operation at an early date. Representatives of the settlers living along the route of this branch went to Montreal and were promised by the railway directors that the line would be in operation in time to carry out the crop of the present year, and in return concessions were made by the settlers in the granting of the right of way. But that branch lias not even been commenced at the present time. When the Bill was in the Railway Committee the representative of the company gave a very definite assurance that the Regina Yorkton branch would be the first branch to be constructed, that the plans were then before the commission and that he expected the work would be commenced in the early part of this summer. That is satisfactory but it would be still more satisfactory if we had a similar promise -with regard to other branches. I again suggest to the government that they should bring pressure to bear on this company to commence work on these branches at tlie earliest possible moment.

When the hon. gentleman from Pictou says this Bill has no relation to tlie construction and operation of the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific, his language is rather extreme. By the statute of 19(K) there are 18 branch lines provided for : One a line from Montreal to a junction with the National Transcontinental Railway ; another a branch line from Montreal, north westerly to a junction with the National Transcontinental Railway ; another branch from Ottawa, another from Regina, another from Prince Albert, another from Calgary, all to junctions with the National Transcontinental Railway, and there is also a branch provided for from a point on the eastern division of the National Transcontinental to St. John or such other port on the Bay of Pundy as may be considered by the company more accessible and better adapted to the purpose of the company. If you look at these branches as being for the purpose of attracting business to and from important centres in the east and west to the National Transcontinental Railway, you wdll see at once the importance of these branch lines and the close relation between their construction and the construction and operation of tlie Grand Trunk Pacific itself.

My hon. friend misapprehended my point. Every one knows these lines which are mentioned in the charter of 1900 are very important propositions involving connection between the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific and business centres in the Dominion. What I intended to say was that under the original charter of the Grand Trunk Pacific and the agreement made with the government certain lines were to be constructed on certain conditions and the company constructing them was to receive certain assistance from the government. The time limit within which these lines were to be completed is fixed in the contract. The point raised by my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) was, that the time limit fixed by this extension would mean that the undertakings in this Bill, which are entirely separate from the others, would not be completed until a time subsequent to that fixed by the original Act. I think I am correct in saying that the proposition to extend the time for completing the undertakings of the Grand Trunk Pacific Branch Lines Company has very little relation to the completion of the undertakings mentioned in the original charter to which government assistance is to be given. I believe the country will regard the extensions proposed in this Bill as eminently reasonable. If the main line and the branches in the original charter are completed in 1910 the large and important branches contemplated in this Act, are completed in 1913, I think the country will be satisfied.

The extension of time asked for here is what is usually granted in ordinary cases and I am not arguing that it is unreasonable. It may be that there will be no detriment to the country if the important branches from Montreal, Ottawa, Regina, Calgary and Prince Albert. have no direct communication immediately with the main line of the Grand Trunk Pacific, for the reason that the main line may not be finished before 1913. It is desirable we should have some information on that point. At what date does the government anticipate that the whole line from Moncton to Prince Rupert will be completed and in operation ? Has the government any information on the subject ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Perhaps the Minister of Railways may have information on this point but 1 have no recent information in regard to it.
Will the Minister of Railways be in soon ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not think he will be here to-day.
Better let the Bill stand until he comes.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Oh, I think not.

Originally when we incorporated this company to build the branch lines, it is apparent from the wording of their Act that we had in view the fact that these branches were to be completed simultaneously with the completion of the main line. Now we extend the time for the building of these, branch lines, but do not extend the time for the building of the main line. Surely this House ought to be informed by the government whether they anticipate that the main line will be finished within the time specified, and if so, what justification is there for extending the time for the building of the branch lines beyond the time when the main line will be completed ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Does not my hon. friend think that this is a matter that can safely be left to the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Company themselves, who are the most interested? For instance, it is of the greatest possible interest to the company to have immediate communication with the city of Montreal. In the same way it is of the greatest possible interest to the company that they should have immediate communication with the various towns in the prairie provinces. It seems to me that we can rest assured that the men in charge of that great enterprise will leave no stone unturned to secure communication with ail these places in order to obtain traffic for the railway at the earliest possible moment.

By the same reasoning you might say that we need not force the company to build branch lines at all, because it is to their interest to have communication with the great cities of the country; but, notwithstanding that, parliament steps in and says you must do so and so. Every company will hold off until it suits its own time and purpose to build, but that may not be for the best interest of the people, and we frequently compel these companies to go beyond what is their own judgment and desire. If the argument of the First Minister is correct, it would relieve this parliament of a great deal of the work we are in the habit of doing from year to year in the way of Mr. R. L. BORDEN.
binding down these companies to do certain things in the interest of the people.
