speechtext: That from and after this date to the end of the session the rule of the House concerning the closing of the sitting on Wednesday at six o'clock, p.m., shall not apply; that from and after this date to the end of the session the House shall meet on every sitting day at eleven o'clock in the morning; that in addition to the usual intermission at six o'clock, p.m., there shall be also an intermission every day from one to three o'clock, p.m.; that government orders shall have precedence at all such sittings, members having still the right to ask questions on Mondays, Wednesdays and Thursdays.

It sems to me that this is a little early for this motion, especially in view of the circumstances at present existing. We have been trying to go through the Order Paper to-day but how many answers have we had to these questions, how many ministers are in their seats? I presume the other ministers are away in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec to run the provincial elections, and there will necessarily be a large number of members out in the country during the present week, or until after the election, in both Ontario and Quebec. In view of that fact I think such a motion would have come very much better after this week because otherwise there will he a great deal of work under consideration of this House and perhaps much of it will be put through which many members who are absent would desire to discuss. It may facilitate the work a little, but there will be the disadvantage of having that work considered by very few members. Much of the work remaining to be done has not yet been placed before the House. The Civil Service Bill and some other Bills have not come down and if they are to be forced through the House in the absence of many members it is not doing justice to the members or to the people.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I have to observe that we are in the seventh month of the session. It is true that the House is 301J
not as full as it might be, but I have not observed of late that the House has taken advantage of the absence of members to rush the work, or to take any precipitate action and therefore I do not see that the complaints of my hon. friend come with any acceptance. If there are any matters that would be likely to suffer from the absence of members, of course they can be postponed until their return. I admit that there are more members absent than I would like but the circumstances are such that gentlemen on neither side of the House can quarrel with them or expect an early return. I hope that next week they will all be in their seats.

The motion is rather unusual in several respects; it proposes to practically abolish one of the rules of the House, that with regard to sittings on Wednesdays, for the remainder of this session. It does not seem to me that this is within the purview of a motion of this kind. We have a Committee on Standing Orders constituted early in the session. It Is not proposed by this resolution to submit the change to the Committee on Standing Orders or any committee, it is simply proposed to abolish more than one of the rules of tlie House for the rest of the session. So far as morning sessions are concerned, that change has been made before and usually without objection. It is to be observed that the second rule of those which were adopted in 1907, provides as follows ;
The time for the ordinary 'meeting of the House is at " o'clock in the afternoon of each sitting d.'.j, xcept Wednesday, when the time of meeting shall be 2 o'clock in the afternoon, and if at the time of meeting there be _ not a quorum, Mr. Speaker may take the Chair and adjourn.
There is express reference there to ordinary meetings of the House, leaving it open to inference at least that we may have an extraordinary sitting of the House at an earlier hour. But the remainder of that second rule is also 'significant.
When the House rises on 'Friday it stands adjourned, unless otherwise ordered, until the following Monday.
An express provision which enables it to be ordered that the House shall sit on Saturday and that Saturday shall be classed as one of the ordinary sitting days of the House.
But the rule in regard to Wednesday evening is couched in very different language. It is as follows :
If at the hour of six o'clock p.m., except on Wednesday, the business of the House be not concluded, Mr. Speaker leaves the Chair until eight o'clock.
At the hour of six o'clock on Wednesday, Mr. Speaker adjourns the House without question put. The House then stands adjourned until Thursday.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council

speechtext: It is provided for in the rule.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Therefore, a Bill can be advanced more than one stage in one day on urgent or extraordinary occasions. But if the occasion is not urgent or extraordinary a Bill cannot be advanced more than one stage in one day without a change of the rule. Rule 52 provides :
Every public Bill shall be read twice in the House before committal or amendment.
This is a standing rule of the House and can be amended the same as others, the same as the rule that the House shall sit at three o'clock.
How do you amend this rule?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: By resolution of this House. That has been done ever since the hon. gentleman came to this parliament, and before. '
The rule as to the three readings?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: The rule that provides that the House shall meet at three o'clock.

I am speaking particularly with reference to the rule providing for three separate readings of a Bill and the variation of the same. He says that that can be amended by the House. In what way?
Sir WILFRID LAURIER, By motion made in this House. Here is the rule :
The itime for the ordinary meeting of the House is at three o'clock in the afternoon of each sitting day except Wednesday, when the time of meeting shall be at 2 o'clock in the afternoon

This rule has neither more or less force than rule 52, for instance. Both are passed by the same authority. Yet ever since the hon. gentleman (Mr. Foster) came to this House, and before either of us came here, this rule which provides for sitting at three o'clock has been amended by resolution of this House to provide that the meeting shall take place at eleven o'clock in the morning. Another rule provides that Saturday shall not be a sitting day. And yet, as my hon. friend knows, a resolution has been passed every session providing that the House shall sit on Saturday. These are all rules of the House for its guidance, and not one has more solemnity or force than any other. If one can be amended by resolution of this House any other can
be amended in the same way. I need not quote precedents, for they are to be found in the records of every session since confederation, as we all know. And, with regard to the motion that I have now made, the same motion was moved by me last year in practically the same words, including a reference to Wednesday evening sittings. On April 2 last year I moved this motion as follows :
That commencing on Wednesday, ithe 3rd of April, to the end of the session, -the rule of the House concerning the closing of the sitting on Wednesday at six o'clock, p.m., shall not apply, and that commencing with the same day, and until the end of the session, the House shall -meet on that day and on each subsequent sitting day at eleven o'clock in the morning; that i-n addition -to -the usual intermission at six o'clock, p.m., there shall be also am -intermission every day from one bo three o'clock, p.m.; that government orders -shall have precedence at all such sittings, members -having still the right -to ask questions on -Mondays, Wednesdays and Thursdays.
I do not know if my bon. friend has refreshed bis memory by reference to the text-book. I have not done so for some time, but X am sure as I can be of anything that the text-books say that the rules of the House are made by the House and can be amended after ordinary notice. As to the propriety of making the motion at the present time, this is a motion to which the House has agreed every session when the business has reached a certain stage. We are now in the seventh month of the session, and I think that the time has come when we may reasonably ask the House to meet in the morning. The only point to be considered is whether it is convenient for the House to do so. The only inconvenience that I can see is in the fact that there is work yet to be done by the committees of the House. All the standing committees with the exception of the Public Accounts Committee have completed their business.
Three Bills were sent to the Private Bills Committee to-day.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: I do not know that they were Bills requiring much attention on the part of the members of this House. They are of a kind, I think, in which we are generally disposed to trust to the judgment of the House from which they come. The Public Accounts Committee has about completed its business.
No, no.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Well, so I have been told, but I speak under correction; it may be that there is more business than I had thought. But let us say that the Public Accounts Committee may still require to sit. The Privileges and Elections Committee which is investigating the

matter of the disappearance of the Stan-stead ballots cannot be called upon to do very heavy work in that connection; it cannot take up much time upon this question. The Quebec bridge investigation and the Hodgins investigation are matters on which I cannot give much information-these are special committees. We must do, as we have done in former sessions, give the committees the privilege of meeting during the sittings of the House.

The point raised by the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) with reference to Wednesday night seems to me to be a new point, and the rule with reference to the recess on Wednesday night sees to be a special rule introduced in the regular manner after consideration by a *committee of this' House appointed to revise the rules. It seems to be rather an absolute rule. The purpose of it was to give an opportunity for members to have a break in the middle of the week's work which they could use for rest and recreation, or, if they chose-as I think moot of the members have chosen-to get up work for the House.
The point is a fairly good one as to whether, if you propose to keep us here night and day to do that work there is not greater need for a break in the middle of the week than there is when you are doing the work in a more leisurely manner. After all the human machine can only do as much as it can do without suffering loss and hardship. The human machine can be tired out as well as any other. When we consider that when the committee which revised the rules thought that it would help the work of parliament to have a break on Wednesday night, so that members might have a chance to recuperate, or at any rate, be relieved from the driving work of the session, it seems to me that there is all the more necessity for a break when you attempt to apply more steam and to work for a greater number of hours per day. I make this plea simply because I am as anxious to get through the work of the House as any one else in the House, but I do not think we will help along the work and certainly not help the workers if we drive the machine unreasonably. I think the Prime Minister will find that he will get just as much work, when the added pressure is put on, by still allowing a break on Wednesday evening as he would if he attempted to keep the members here every day, day and night, two sessions in the day time and one in the evening with the attendant tiring and wearying. My right hon. friend knows what always happens when a deliberative, controversial assembly, besides having the objects of controversy before it, comes to them with tired brains, tired minds and tired tempers. I put that point before the Prime Minister and I would like to see him leave the Wednesday night out Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
of the motion and still allow, for the present at least, that break. I believe that better business would be done in the House and that the motion would be more effective.
In reference to putting on the pressure at this time of the session, Mr. Speaker, if you take the government business alone, some of which we have before us and some of which we have not before us, the government business alone, ir it is to be fairly met and fairly canvassed and if legislators are to do their duty, cannot be done in a week, or two weeks, or three weeks. See what there is. Take your Election Bill and, after June 8, when the Prime Minister comes to the conclusion that it is no longer necessary to push those obnoxious clauses and we go into the Bill as a whole, does not the Prime Minister see that if we are going to perform the promises that have been held out for five years with reference to a pure election Bill, there will be clauses to be enacted and certainly clauses to be discussed which will take time ? It is impossible to put the Bill through with even the provisions that are anticipated in the Bill and the provisions in the Bill which were proposed by my hon. friend from Prince Edward county (Mr. Alcorn) and which are to be debated, without a great deal of discussion and a great deal of talk. Going to the country, as we are supposed to do under this new election Bill, we want the very best kind of a Bill and we want one which will promote the purity of elections and do away with the old abuses.
Then, you have not yet explained to the House probably a still mo.e important Bill in its way than the Election Bill; that is the Civil Service Bill, I do not know what other members think of it, but for myself it seems to me that when we approach the making of a Civil Service Bill under the present conditions in Canada we are undertaking a great deal of labour which will not be well done if there is great haste, and if there is an inordinate pressure put upon the House. Yet here we are, as the Prime Minister says, in the seventh month of the session and we have not yet had the provisions of the Civil Service Bill explained to us. The Bill has not even been presented to the House. Some intimations have been received by members of the press as to what its provisions may be expected to be, but the House does not know and the country does not know. That is not the fault of the opposition at all and the Prime Minister must not put on his double and treble pressure with the idea of making the opposition foot up because of the long and inexcusable delay of the ministry in bringing down one of the most important Bills that has not yet been introduced in this the seventh month of the session. There is the Hudson's Bay railway ; we have had an intimation in reference to it but we have no statement as to when this

measure will be brought down. It is not yet before the House. That will be an important Bill and the important question of ways and means, involving a great obligation on this country, has to be discussed. Then there is the Land Bill of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Oliver) which has just been introduced and which also is a fertile question of discussion. But, there is no use of mentioning others. Nearly all of the government legislation is as yet barely explained or unexplained in the seventh month of the session, and there is work to be done which requires better consideration than that which can be be given to it by jaded members working from 11 o'clock in the morning until midnight, as the right hon. Prime Minister proposes. Then, go to the work of the committees, which is just as important in its way as the work in the House. The Public Accounts Committee has business now before it to keep the members of the committee at work for a month or a month and a half, and it is almost impossible to do satisfactory work with committees and the House going on at the same time. There is the Committee on Banking and Commerce. That committee has had one wrestle with the Insurance Bill but that was only a preliminary wrestle. That committee does not yet know what the Bill is to be. It has simply heard the objections and heard the pleas, but it has not dealt with the Bill itself and everybody knows that the Insurance Bill is one of a controversial nature, and you cannot put it through in a day. The government saw lit to send it to the committee, but not a single clause of that Bill has as yet been put before that committee for discussion. We have simply had the hearings from the different societies and individuals who are interested in one or other of the phases of that Bill But, the Banking and Commerce Committee has not yet commenced the discussion of that Bill. It has to go through it clause by clause, the Bill has to be reported to the House and then it becomes government legislation coming before the House in the seventh or eight month of the session. That is an important committee and it is an important Bill which has to be threshed out. Taking all these things into consideration, taking into consideration the fact which was well put forth by my hon. friend from East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that, not of our own fault, we are in the throes of two provincial elections-one would have been enough, but the friends of the Prime Minister thought it would be better to have two .going on at the same time and so they brought on the elections in the province of Quebec on the same date as those upon which the elections in Ontario are being held-i very much question the wisdom of the right hon. gentleman's motion. These elections take out the very strongest members from each side of the House. Do you
propose this week to rush legislation of that important nature through the House when many hon. members are out of the House and when these contests are going on ? These are considerations which I thought would appeal to the Prime Minister and my suggestion would be that the Prime Minister do not put this into force for this week at any rate, and that if he does put it in force next week ne should not cut out the Wednesday night recess. I am not objecting to trying to get through the work of the House just as quickly as possible;
I want to do it. I would like to have a good long holiday before the elections come on and we cannot get that unless we can get through some time before the first of August.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I quite agree with my hon. friend from North Toronto (Mr. Foster) that there is a very considerable volume of legislation before the House, but I draw from that condition quite the opposite conclusion that my hon. friend has drawn. In a well organized factory, when the orders accumulate, the general rule is to work extra time and do the work.
This is not a well organized factory.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is fairly well organized, except that it has always been assumed that hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House would recognize their responsibilities and that the machinery would go on, but, it seems that there has been an erroneous impression in that respect. We cannot help that. But the rule in a well organized factory, when business increases, is to put on the hands for extra hours. They pay them extra. I do not suppose that we would expect an extra indemnity by reason of working extra hours, but I think the country will expect that if the factory at Ottawa is to do the business which is before it it should work extra hours.
The factory usually puts on extra hands.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
It seems to me that if the number of hands were not sufficient that would be a good reason for working extra hours. My hon. friend (Mr. Foster) has alluded to the Wednesday evening meeting. I must say that the Wednesday evening adjournment is rather dear to my heart. I had the honour of proposing that to the committee ; I was the author of it. Early in the session we work along in a moderately easy way, but after we have passed the six months I think the public opinion of the country will say it Is time that parliament may reasonably be called ujion to work longer hours and finish its work. While I am a strong advocate of the Wednesday evening recess, still I would think that at this advanced stage of the session we

should relinquish it, and that we might work on Saturdays also close up to the hour when the Sabbath commences. It is true important Bills are yet to be brought forward, but that does not imply neglect on the part of the government, because there could be no object infringing forward other legislation when no progress is being made with the volume of business already before; the House. Important as these measures are to which reference has been made, the most important work of this House at present is the work of voting supplies for carrying on the King's government. In our judgment that is the most important, work which this House requires to do now, and it is with the object of expediting this, and to prevent the embarrassment which will arise if there be delay in voting supplies, that we ask the House to put its utmost energy into the work before it.. There has never been a moment from the first day of the session down to the present hour when there has not been an abundant programme of government business before the House, and if that programme has not been advanced more rapidlv than some of us desired, we certainly believe it Is not the fault of the government.

There is yet a great deal of important work to be done in the Public Accounts Committee and the members of that committee cannot attend to it and to their duties in the House at the same time. To-day is nomination day for the provincial elections and there are a great many members absent who were they present would strongly protest against this proposal of the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance have said that we were near the end of this session.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I did not say that.

The Prime Minister said that such a motion as this was customary when we came towards the end of the session, but there is an impression in my part of the country that we are not half through the session yet, and certainly if we do not make better progress than we have in the past that idea is perfectly correct. The Minister of Finance says it is important that the estimates be passed, but I am inclined to think it fortunate that these estimates have not been rushed through in view of the financial conditions which face the country. The revenue last month showed a decrease of one and three quarter million dollars as compared with the corresponding month of last year, and in my judgment that condition will continue for some time. I regret that the business of the country is bad and I hope it will improve. but my opinion is that there will not be very much improvement this year. I have great confidence in the future of the country, but still we must look forward to a decreasing revenue, and it is therefore Mr. FIELDING.
necessary to carefully criticise these estimates. Indeed it may be advisable for the government to cut the expenditures down. Then there is the Insurance Bill and the Banking and Commerce Committee have not finished its work and cannot finish its work properly if there are to be morning sittings. I thought this session was to be a sort of Insurance Bill session, but we have treated it very lightly so far and justice cannot be done to it now. There is the Civil Service Bill and there is the Election Bill, and there are twenty-two other government measures on the drder Paper. All these matters must receive careful consideration. While it may be necessary to pass such a motion as this in the closing wTeeks of the session, this is not the proper time to present it. In view of the fact that so many members are absent to-day and will be absent during the coming week, the time is inopportune for the Prime Minister to propose this motion, and I would urge on him that he should leave it over for at least a week.

I think the rrime Minister is unfair to the members of this House and especially to the members of the opposition in trying to press this motion at this stage. Such a motion is usually made during the last two or three weeks of the session, but even if one or two of the most contentious measures proposed by the government were dropped entirely, there is sufficient on the Order Paper and sufficient work promised by the gov-ment to take up the time of the House for at least six weeks longer. Suppose the Election Act were entirely withdrawn I do not see how it would be possible to finish the work of the session in less than six weeks from this date. Last year the Prime Minister made a similar motion on the 3rd of April and parliament prorogued on the 28th but I am quite sure there will be no prorogation this year *within the next month. The Finance Minister has said that the most important thing for the House to do at present is to pass the estimates, which looks as if we would have supply every day this week. It is the members on this side of the House who most largely discuss the estimates.
Hear, hear.

The hon. gentleman says ' hear, hear,' but are not the members supporting the government interested in seeing the expenditures of this country properly criticised? They ought to be interested but in practice they would vote $90,000,000 in two hours if they had their way, so long as it went to their own constituencies. It is rarely we hear adverse criticism of the estimates from members on the other side and as many hon. gentlemen will be absent during the coming week, any proposal to rush through legislation and es-

timates without proper criticism cannot be defended. It is not the fault of the opposition that the session has been long. The government promised several Bills in the speech from the Throne and these Bills have not yet seen the light of day. The Boundary Bill for the province of Manitoba was promised but it has not been submitted to the House yet. I do not know what the character of the Bill may be, but I do say that if it does not meet with the wishes of the people of the west it will prove to be a most contentious measure. Then there is the voluminous and contentious Land Bill of the Minister of the Interior which was left - over last session and which was brought down only last week. .That Bill will require a great deal of discussion. If we are to have morning sessions and if there is no guarantee that we will not have to sit until long after midnight as was the case during the last two weeks, then I say the proposal is unfair to the members of the opposition. Hon. gentlemen on both sides of the House are engaged in the Ontario and Quebec provincial elections this week ; they no doubt believe they are fighting the battle of their country in their respective constituencies, and I do not think we should be compelled to recall our forces from these provinces in order to properly criticise legislation. The Prime Minister is very unfair in bringing this resolution forward when so many members of the House are absent. I was not a very enthusiastic supporter of the Wednesday night holiday, but, after having had some experience of it, and knowing how beneficial it is to members who do not spend the time in social functions, as many of us do not, to have this opportunity to prepare, their work for the balance of the week, I for one, think that if this motion passes, the Wednesday night sittings should be omitted. Personally I enter my earnest protest against this motion passing at the present time. I think we shall do as much work if the Prime Minister postpones it for another week, when all the members will be here, and supply and the various matters of legislation that are to come forward, will receive a fair amount of criticism.

It is almost impossible to understand the arguments of hon. gentlemen opposite; for they dwell on the large quantity of work that is to be done before this session's conclusion, and from that premiss they argue that we should stop working or do as little as we possibly can. They tell us that we should not sit'in the mornings or on Wednesdays, or indeed at any time unless we cannot help it. We are informed that our constituents all over the country are getting up earlier in the morning and working later at night at this season of the year in their ordinary avocations, and they naturally believe that their representatives in parliament ought to
be at least as assiduous in attending to the public business of this country. But when we are told by hon. gentlemen opposite that there is a great deal of work to be done and that therefore we should stop working, one is rather at a loss to understand them. I am surprised that my hon. friend from East Toronto (Mr. Kemp), who very rarely honours this House with his presence, and whose attendance on the committees is even more rare
Entirely mistaken.

MACDONALD-should take that position. As one who comes from a distant province, and who has some business interests at home-and there are, I am sure, a great many members in the same position -<1 feel that the time has come in this session when every member of the House should apply himself with the greatest possible assiduity to the public business in order that the session should be brought to an end. After six or seven months absence from home, I think we have reached a stage when we should give up our Wednesday evenings, and get up earlier in the morning in order to get the public business attended to. Hon. gentlemen who can go home for a day or two at any period of the session, and whose business interests are not suffering by their attendance at parliament, can very easily talk about taking things easily; but members from distant provinces are not in that position, and it is by the greatest possible sacrifice of our business interests that we are kept here so long. The hon. member for East Toronto, in expressing his desire to scrutinize the estimates more closely, is at variance with the whip of the party, who said the other night that they would pass these estimates in a few minutes if certain things were done.
What did he say?
He was perfectly willing to pass all the estimates in a few minutes if something was done that suited him.
No, he was not.
This is what the whip of the party said, as you will find if you look at ' Hansard ' on page 9529 ;
They will not go through now. Let the government withdraw clauses 1 and 17 of the Election Bill, and they will get their estimates in a very few iminutes.
Is not the hon. gentleman aware that it was only the estimates then before the House, not the whole of the estimates, that he referred to?

My hon. friend from Dufferin has developed a great deal of wisdom and inscrutable knowledge since lie has been in this House, and he seems to be able to tell us what the hon.

member for Leeds was thinking about. As a rule, we are accustomed to take words spoken in the House as meaning exactly what they say, and the words of the hon. member for Leeds indicated the most delightful willingness on the part of himself and his hon. friend to pass all the estimates of this government in a few minutes if something were done that suited him. I am surprised, therefore, that the hon. member for East Toronto, who does not honour the House with his genial presence very often, and who has manifested such a strong desire to scrutinize the estimates, should be at variance with the gentleman who whips him and the other hon. gentlemen on that side of the House. In regard to the work still to be done, our hon. friends have somewhat exaggerated the work still before the committees. Hon. gentlemen who attend the Public Accounts Committee will agree with me, I think, that the work of that committee has been very long and laboured, and that to-day only the fag-end of it remains. Indeed, it has sat for two or three days dealing with matters that ought not to be before that committee at all. From the order paper and from the expressions of opinion given informally by hon. gentlemen opposite in the committee, there cannot be much work left for it to do. At any rate, there is no reason why hon. gentlemen should not apply themselves more assiduously at this season of the year and at this stage of the session to the public business of this country in order that it should be closed up as speedily as possible. The country expects it of us. The busy people^ of this country expect their representatives to attend to their business It seems to me that the motion of the right hop. leader of the House .is not made a moment too soon, and that the House should in its own interest and in the interest of the country adopt it.

My hon. friend says that he cannot understand the arguments of hon. gentlemen on this side of the House. All I can say is that they are very clear and lucid, and if he cannot understand them, we cannot undertake to supply him with brains for that purpose. With reference to the statement of our whip, he distinctly stated that if hon. gentlemen opposite would do away with the obnoxious Election Bill, which I venture to say has shocked not only the members of this House, on both sides but the country at large, we would pass these estimates, that is, the estimates then before the House.
Oh, no; read the words.

I have read them, and the hon. gentleman can read them at his leisure. As the discussion of the estimates is the only power we have in our hands, we are quite justified if we take longer time Mr. MACDONALD.
than is necessary under these circumstances; and I venture to say that nine-tenths of the free and independent electors of Canada, from the Atlantic to the Pacific, will say that the opposition are only doing their duty in fighting that obnoxious Bill by any power within their reach. With regard to the motion before the House, I venture to say that if you look over the history of the Dominion of Canada, you will not find any parallel case, either in the Dominion parliament or in any provincial parliament, in *which the members are asked to double up their work, and work night and day at this stage of the business. It does not matter how loug we have beeu here. If we have been six months, we cannot help that. The country demands that we as its representatives scrutinize not only the estimates, but every Bill that comes before the House, whether it takes six months or eight months or the rest of the year; and while we are all desirous of shortening the session as much as possible, we feel that we have a dutyMo our country and our constituents. Medical men at any rate know that we cannot scrutinize the estimates or the legislation that comes before this House as well if we spend twenty hours of the day at work, as we could if we took a reasonable rest; and in my opinion more progress would be made if we went on in the even tenor of our way, at least for the present, working reasonable hours. When we look at the amount of work still before us, we cannot come to any other conclusion than that the session has just commenced, because the work to be done is much more than the work we have accomplished during the past six months; and if we have to spend the rest of the year here, it is only our duty to do so, however anxious we may be to return to our homes. It is an utter impossibility to shorten the work by compelling the members to work under greater pressure for three or four months. In my opinion the present is not an opportune time for bringing in a motion of this kind, as the members from Ontario and Quebec are necessarily absent.
Many members from Ontario and Quebec are necessarily away, and so far as Quebec is concerned, the hon. gentlemen opposite are responsible for their absence as we know that if the mandate had not gone down from here the elections in Quebec would not be on to-day. But, the government, knowing the defeat that stares them in the face in Ontario, the sweep that will be made there a week from to-day, felt that Quebec might and as we believe will follow suit although probably not to the same extent. But still the government said: Let us have the downfall all together, and then the country will not have two opportunities of passing judgment upon us. Under these circumstances, the government may well move carefully until they see the result of the elections and probably they

may change their minds as far as that obnoxious Bill is concerned and become more reasonable in many things. I believe they are heartily ashamed of sections 1 and 17 of the Election Bill and are anxious to get out of it in some way. They could do this very easily if they waited until after the provincial elections. Then probably if they desire it we will work longer hours. Under these circumstances I think it would be in the interest of the House if at least the Wednesday night should not be taken away and also if one week respite should be given before starting the morning sessions.

Mr. Speaker, I am rather surprised at the speech of the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. E. M. Macdonald). He never rises without indulging in personalities and usually manages to place a very false construction on statements made. I shall not follow him in his personalities but I wish to correct his construction of statements of hon. gentlemen on this side. We have never suggested that there should be a stoppage of work altogether or additional holidays. All we have done is to protest against the proposal of the government being adopted at this moment, when there is such an enormous amount of work yet to be done. The hon. gentleman spoke of our constituents who are putting in very much longer hours of work than are members of this House. The hon. member could not have been quite serious iu that suggestion or else he must have forgotten that there are committees of this House which meet practically every morning in the week, and that in addition there is a great deal of correspondence to which every member has to attend. The hours of work of members of parliament are far in excess of those of almost any other class of the population of Canada.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) puts some blame on the opposition for the delays which have taken place in connection with some legislation which has been brought before the House. But we must remember that the insurance legislation, which will require the very serious consideration of this House and previous to that the serious consideration of the Committee on Banking and Commerce, has not yet come before that committee for their consideration and report, and this surely is not the fault of the opposition but of the government. The Prime Minister has said that we are in the seventh month of the session. That carries with it the further thought that after we have been in session for six months the government has not yet brought down an important measure which was promised in the speech from the Throne, the Manitoba Boundaries Bill which is likely to cause a very large amount of discussion. Then again only within the last few days has that important and very contentious Bill the Dominion Lands Act been brought down.
These and the Civil Service and other Bills which the government have promised, have not yet been brought down and they will have to be gone into very thoroughly by every member if we are to get the best legislation possible under the circumstances.
I do not see how this will be possible if we are to attend to committee meetings in the mornings and also to our correspondence. If the Prime Minister had included a provision that the House should rise at midnight each night there might have been a better disposition on the part of members towards his proposal, but we know that members will be kept busy from 9.30 in the morning until perhaps 3 or 4 the next morning with the usual short intermissions for luncheon and dinner. It seems to me to be not quite fair to the members. I would point out that from the wording of the motion, taken iu connection with the rules of the House, there would appear to be no intermission for dinner on Wednesday evening.
I hope that the Prime Minister will agree to an amendment which I propose to move as follows :
That the said motion he amended by striking out the words'* from and after this date * wherever they occur therein, and by substituting therefor in each ease the words * from and after Monday next.'
That, at any rate will give an additional week for the members of the House to come in. from the various districts in Ontario and Quebec where so many of them are to-day performing what are after all very important duties.

I desire to endorse what has been said by members on this side, certainly with regard to tbe evening recess on Wednesday. If it is intended to force the work of the House morning, afternoon and evening, certainly the Wednesday evening recess is more important at this time in relation to the health of members alone than in the earlier part of the session when members are not so pressed and so much driven with work. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has given a clear statement of the number of government Bills that have not yet been presented. There are several Bills not yet introduced, government measures, which it is to be presumed, the government intend to press. It looks a good deal like coercion, like tyranny, for the Prime Minister and members on the government side, at such a time as this, especially, with so many members of the House absent, to force such a proposal as this upon members affecting their attendance in the House. Members will be expected to assemble at eleven o'clock in the morning and to remain here all day,-and at wliat time late at night or early in tbe morning the House will adjourn nobody can tell ; if tbe practice is

continued which has held for some time in the past, it will be two, or three, or foul-o'clock in the morning before members leave this House.- How can it be expected that we'can give that attention to measures coming before the House, whether estimates or Bills, that we should give if we are kept at such high pressure of work as the Prime Minister proposes ? I think it ought only be necessary to bring these points to the attention of the leader of the House to have him forego his intention of pressing this motion at this time. The amendment to postpone this proposal for a week's time, I think, is asking little enough. At least, we may expect that, after this week more members will be in harness here and the work can be divided, thus relieving the pressure upon each member. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald), who is always interesting in his remarks though somewhat imaginative as to facts, referred to a remark made the other night by the hon. member for Heeds (Mr. Taylor). That hon. member is now in his place and will be able to explain what he really meant when he said that if certain action was taken with regard to the Elections Bill the estimates would be put through in two minutes. I am sure that he referred only to the item then before the committee. But, as he is here, he will be able to explain. I once more appeal to the Prime Minister and his supporters to allow this motion to be postponed for a week. If at that time it is considered necessary to bring it in again, the members on both sides will be in a better position to share the irksome work which long hours of attendance in this House will involve.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Whenever this motion is made, the intention of the government is to try to meet the wishes of members on both sides, and I do not approach the consideration of the matter in any other spirit to-day. I was impressed with the statements made by several hon. members, particularly by the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) as to the value of the recess on Wednesday evening. Therefore, if it be agreeable to my hon. friend on the other side, I will move an amendment to the amendment that the first words of the motion, relating to Wednesday evening, shall not apply. I do not say but that later on, if the work presses, we may be obliged to propose Wednesday evening sittings, but, for the present, we will give hon. gentlemen the advantage of the rest on Wednesday evenings.
I think that is a fair proposition.

Perhaps, I misunderstood the Prime Minister. Does he propose Mr. DANIEL.
to abandon the idea of Wednesday night sittings ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: To leave the rule as to Wednesday as it is.
And to apply the rest of the motion ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

I frankly confess that I do not feel like agreeing with that. So far as it goes, it is right enough, but I wish to make one or two observations on the proposition. The motion for morning sittings is generally made when practically all the committee work of the session is ended. So long as the commttees have work in hand, the forenoon is needed by hon. members to attend to that work and to correspondence. The First Minister says he made this motion last year at a certain time. But when he made it, practically all the committee work was over. Is that the position to-day ? I think there is scarcely a committee of this House which has finished its work. A number of important committees are engaged in their work as vigourously now as at any time during the session. The Public Accounts Committee has enough to do for three months, should the session last that long ; and the committee will have to work with greater expedition than hitherto if they are to get through by the time the session may be expected to close. As to the Private Bills Committe, we sent to-day four Bills to that committee to consider. The Prime Minister intimated that these are divorce Bills on which not much time is spent by the committee. But I can remember divorce Bills coming before that committee on which witnesses were called and a great deal of time spent.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Invading the privileges of the Senate.

We have the same right to call witnesses as the Senate have. I remember that, in the case of one Bill that was before us some years ago we called witnesses some of whom had not been called before the Senate Committee. And the Private Bills Committee may decide to do the same in the case of some of these Bills which are now sent for their consideration. Then we have business before the Privileges and Elections Committee. I assume that it will not take them very long to dispose of that work. Still, it takes a week or ten days to deal with almost any cases that may come before the committee. There are still some Bills to go before the Committee on Railways, Canals and Telegraph Lines, Then, as the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) has said, if the Banking and Commerce

Committee is to deal with the Insurance Bill at all every clause of that Important measure must come under the consideration of the committee. The Banking and Commerce Committee has a large membership, and those who are members of it will desire to carefully consider the insurance Bill clause by clause. And we have had no intimation that that Bill is not to go on ; the assumption is that it will go on. We have the committee on Agriculture and Colonization-that committee also has not finished its work. As to the Hodgins inquiry, I was told by the hon. member for South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) the other day that it is likely to continue for a week or ten days, or two weeks, as far as he can judge, although the committee are hurrying the business on. The Quebec Bridge inquiry will take a considerable length of time if any thing like a proper investigation is made. With all these committees engaged in important work, it must be that a large number of members will be occupied in the forenoon. How is it possible for the House to go on with its regular work at eleven o'clock when so many members who ought to be here are engaged in committees ? Sometimes the rule is suspended and committees are allowed to go on with their work while this House is sitting. That is an injustice to members of the House and to the country, as ail members ought to be present when business is before us. Besides that, during the present week-during which it is proposed that this motion be left in abeyance-more than half the members are likely to be absent. I counted the attendance here a short time ago and, all told, only forty members were present. Is it reasonable that the business of this House should be carried on with less than one-fifth of the membership of the House in attendance ? I contend that it would be much more reasonable to carry out the suggestion I made some time ago and have this House adjourn for a week until the pending elections are over.
A large number of members will be absent and the important work that ought to be considered by all the members cannot be considered when three-fourths of them are absent as they are during the present week. In addition to that, and in addition to the committee work, to force this on during this week when there will not be one-fifth of the members present, is an injustice to the country and it is performing the functions of parliament in a very improper way. The motion is a very improper one. The hon. member for Pic-tou (Mr. Macdonald) intimated that the business of the House is not going on very actively, that it is rather retai'ded. I would like to ask him if there is any member of this House who has contributed more to
retarding the proper and legitimate business of the House than the hon. gentleman himself? I have sat in the Public Accounts Committee day after day when we did not do as much work in a week as we ought to have done in a day. About three members obstruct the work of that committee, and he was one of the most active in doing it. Had the members of that committee been able to do their work as they ought to have been without any improper interference or obstruction, the work would not be, as it is to-day-only partially done. It would have been comparatively all done and we would have been in a position to abandon it and apply ourselves to the work of this House. Owing to the special situation to-day this motion should not be pushed. It is a fact that these committees have not their work done, they have a large amount of important work to be done and until that work is done ' the House cannot properly sit in the forenoon, or otherwise the committees cannot do their work. You are taking men away from the House who ought to be here for the consideration of important Bills and estimates. We ought to have a delay for at least one week. Then the Prime Minister ought to consider whether we would not be just as far on with the business in two or three weeks hence if we adjourned the House for one week until these elections are over. I do not believe it would be doing justice to the country to push this work through when so many members are away, and I do not think it would retard the progress of the session much if we were to adjourn. Members would then be present and be able to attend to their work. In view of these features of it I would respectfully urge upon the First Minister that it is not enough to abandon the proposal to take Wednesday night, but that it is eminently proper and desirable that this motion should be delayed for one week until the members have returned.

One point which is very material to be considered seems to me to have been almost lost sight of. It was possibly referred to in general terms at the beginning of the debate, but it has not been mentioned since, and that is whether the House has the right to pass a motion of this kind if it be objected to by a substantial number of members, if not by one member. Let me draw attention to the fact that the rules of the House contain no provision for the abrogation or even suspension of any of its rules, and if one rule may be suspended or abrogated the whole of them may be by the same motion. They contain no provision for the abrogation or suspension of any one rule except under certain circumstances with regard to private Bills. Clearly if, on a motion not unanimously assented to, any one standing order of the House may be sus-

pended or abrogated, we might wipe out the whole body of them by a bare majority. I think the Prime Minister will probably do well to carefully consider that point and withhold his motion until lie is satisfied that upon a motion which is not unanimously agreed to, but which is seriously objected to, he can suspend a rule of the House.

I was not present, but 1 have been informed since I came in that the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) made the statement that I said a few nights ago that if the government would withdraw clauses 1 and 17 of the Election Act they would get their whole estimates through in two minutes. I certainly did not say that in the light in which the hon. gentleman puts it. We were then discussing the estimates of the hon. Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) and I made the suggestion that if these clauses were withdrawn he could have the pay for the men for whom he was making his appeal in a couple of minutes. I believe that the opposition have allowed since I have been absent from the House this amount to pass through. But I made no reference to the general estimates that are yet to come down. It was simply because of the appeals that have been made to us by the Minister of Customs. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), during the debate, threw the taunt across the floor of the House that the opposition had been obstructing business for the last six months. That cannot possibly be the fact, because if you take up ' Hansard ' and measure it you will find that hon. members supporting the government have occupied more than half of the 1 Hansard ' from the commencement of the session up to the present time.
What will you bet?

I am not a betting man, but I will make the statement that if my hon. friend takes the ' Hansard ' and measures it he will find that the government and their supporters have occupied a greater number of pages than the opposition have done during the entire session. Therefore, we are not to be taunted with having obstructed because there have been many valuable speeches made from this side of the House to enlighten the country. Read these speeches made by members of the opposition and compare them with the balderdash we have heard from the other side of the House-nothing but trash, save and except a few speeches made by members of the government. But those speeches made by the back benchers bear no comparison with the brilliant speeches made upon this side of the House. Yet the hon. Minister of Finance gets up and taunts us with obstructing the House. All the speeches from this side have been made to educate the people of the country and the people of the country have been Mr. ALCORN.
educated, but the speeches made from the opposite side of the House were simply to obstruct or kill time and to show that the Conservative government was as bad as the present government twelve or fifteen years ago. But we are not to be charged with having obstructed this House for six months or even one month. We have an objection and we are going to maintain our objection. I went back to my constituents and they told me to stay here until Christmas if it were necessary to have eliminated the inquity of clauses 1 and 17 of the Election Bill. My constituents are witling to raise a subscription to pay my board if necessary to keep me here until Christmas in order to see that the ballot shall not be tampered with and that the province of Manitoba shall not be singled out. Manitoba is peopled mostly by the sons of Ontario, Quebec and the maritime provinces, the men who opened up and developed that country, and now, because this government, through the North Atlantic Trading Company, have transported into that country a lot of Doukhobors and-

speechtext: Order.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. gentleman (Mr. Taylor) is wandering a little too far from the subject.

I saw in the newspapers that the right hon. gentleman had given notice that he was going to take Wednesday night. I have no objection to take Wednesday night commencing at a reasonable hour in the day. I do not think that any one objects, if the rule can be broken. In order to expedite the business I would be willing that the government should take Wednesday with the condition that we commence at eleven o'clock in the day, as soon as the committee work is through, and continue until twelve o'clock at night and not be forced to sit until five o'clock in the morning as we were last week. I do not think our constituents expeet us to remain here until five o'clock in the morning as it must be injurious to the health of every hon. member who is confined to this box of a chamber-it is nothing else-from three o'clock in the afternoon until five the next morning. I think it is dangerous to the health of every hon. member, but I would be willing, if my hon. friend the leader of the opposition (Mr. R. L. Borden) and the right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) agree to it, to give up Wednesday night provided we sit until twelve or one o'clock.
How do you feel on the customs estimates now?
Just as I felt the other night.
In two minutes.

Oh, well, the Minister of Customs got a portion of his estimates with-

out dropping clauses 1 and 17 of the Election Bill, as I wanted him to do. He made such a strong appeal to our leader that I understand he consented to pay the boys in the outside service. But we have lots of more estimates to pass yet.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Lots of them.
I did not get all mine.
Just whenever the Prime Minister carries out the bargain there will be no obstruction of the estimates so far as I am concerned.

I wish to correct the statement made by the hon. member for Leeds when he said that the greater part of the time of this House has been taken up by members supporting the government. I had the curiosity to figure up the number of columns of ' Hansard ' which were occupied by the debate on the Election Bill and I find that the members of the opposition are eighty-two columns ahead. If they don't believe me they can count it up for themselves.
My hon. friend cannot contradict me because I referred to the whole session and not to the debate on one Bill.	.

And if you count it up you will get the same result for the entire
session.
Well, do not contradict me until you do count.
The hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Roche) took sixty-three columns of ' Hansard ' in that debate.
And he did it in about half the time that some of your men took, so that no time was lost there.

If some of the hon. gentlemen who have spoken on the other side of the House were in the position that I and other members from the far west are in they would be glad to adopt any means to bring the session to a close. We have been six months away from our homes and our business; we cannot run home every week and attend to our private affairs as can the hon. member for Leeds and others who live near Ottawa. We have to leave our business aside for months to attend to the business of the country and we would like to see the country's business disposed of in a businesslike way. I cannot for the life of me understand how it is that this House can be held up by a minority. That puzzles me. I always understood that one of the fundamental rules of our constitution was that we should have government by majority, government by the people and for the people. Each one of us here is returned by a majority of the votes in our
constituencies and why the majority in this House cannot rule is something that I don't understand. So far as the Election Bill is concerned there is supposed to be a deadlock in connection with it

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: I think it would be well to confine the discussion to the question before the House.

Well, I was a little afraid 1 would be out of order, but so many others have offended in that respect that 1 thought I would be quite safe in doing so too. However, I will give my views on that question at another time.

When the hon. member for Pictou complained about the long hours he is devoting to the interests of the country and the hardship of his being away from his home it reminded me of a statement made by the sitting member who was seeking re-election in a constituency in Prince Edward Island, and when he made the same complaint about long hours in parliament and the misfortune of his being absent from his private business, an elector at the back of the hall called out:	You
have done so much in that line that you had better stay at home altogether next time. Now. Mr. Speaker, there are a great many-important measures before the House and there is a great deal of important business to be transacted by the committees, and in view of this the motion of the Prime Minister is inopportune and unreasonable especially as only about one-fifth of the members of the House are present to-day. These gentlemen are in their constituencies in Ontario and Quebec attending to the interests of the country in the provincial elections and I believe the people of Canada will look upon it that the Prime Minister is unfair in taking advantage of the existing conditions, especially in view of the fact that there is to some extent a deadlock between the parties on account of the injustice which the government is trying to force on the nrovinee of Manitoba. I think the Prime Minister might very well accept the amendment of the hon. member for Qu'Ap-pelle.

The Prime Minister has been very reasonable with reference to the Wednesday night recess, and I have no doubt his decision in that respect will be helpful to the convenience of the House. If the right hon. gentleman would consent to allow this motion only to come into effect on Monday next I think it would contribute to the good nature and the good work of the whole House. It would also tend to facilitate the work of the committees and I think it would be a reasonable concession for the right hon. gentleman to make.

The motion of the Prime Minister is inopportune and it is especially

inopportune if it is to come into effect before next week. There is a great deal of work to be done in the Public Accounts Committee and it is inexpedient that that committee should sit during the morning sittings of the House. I believe the right hon. gentleman would better serve the end he desires to achieve by not pressing this resolution at present. Am I right in assuming that the original motion is amended by striking out the words from the first word * that ' in the first line down to and including the word ' apply ' in the third line ?

x take it that the amendment is still before the House.
_ Mr. SPEAKER. I understood the amendment was to be dropped and the original motion amended.
The amendment to the amendment was that the original motion be amended in that direction.

Very good, with that understanding; but the motion will have to be made at some time or another.

The amendment to the motion is still before the House-to suspend this for a week.

Mr. FIELDING moved that the House go into Committee of Supply.

I wish to bring before the attention of the House the question of the duty on lumber coming from the United States into Canada. It is not my intention tonight to propose a motion on the matter or to bring on a general discussion ; my object in bringing it up is to direct the attention of the government to the existing condition of affairs in the hope that they will see their way clear to remedy the existing grievance. If this is not done then we might feel in duty bound to take the matter up at a later stage of the session and to press it more closely upon the attention of the government. At the present time lumber

from the United States or any foreign country enters Canada free of duty. On rough lumber from Canada to the United States there is a duty of $2 a thousand feet which is a practical handicap upon the Canadian lumber entering that country. The industry in Canada to-day employs between 65,000 and 75,000 men, according to the season, represents a population of about 300,000 to 400,000 souls, depending upon the lumber industry in Canada for a livelihood. . Not only are these directly concerned in the lumber industry, but indirectly the financial institutions of the country, the railways, the mercantile, manufacturing and farming communities all doing business with the lumbermen, are all very deeply interested in the success of that industry. In addition to those X have named as persons employed in the industry exclusively there are a great many farmers' sons and labouring men in all parts of the country who, when the winter approaches, having no work at home on the farms during the long period of winter, find employment in the lumber camps at the nearest point where there are lumbering operations, travelling sometimes hundreds of miles to obtain work. So these are employed indirectly for a period of six months or so every year in the lumber woods.
In order to show the growth of the import of lumber, I would point out that in 1908, the year just closed, there were" imported into the Dominion of Canada lumber and lumber materials of the value of $12,730,000. The total product of the Dominion of Canada is estimated this year to be considerably less than $100,000,000. Therefore about one dollar's worth was imported to each eight dollars manufactured in Canada. The value of the imports of lumber from the United States increased from $2,904,000 in 1896 to the enormous sum of $12,730,000 in the present year. Of that $12,730,000, $2,800,000 was dutiable and $9,930,000 free.
The wages paid to lumbermen in the district which I have the honour to represent a year ago were $35 a month. They have now fallen to between $20 and $25 a month, and there is every reason to believe that in the very near future the wages will fall still lower. Therefore we have an army of about 70,000 able bodied men with their families who are entitled to live in decency in Canada on the verge of being reduced upwards of fifty per cent in their wages. More than that, very many of these men are being turned out of employment. It is a very serious matter in many parts of the country.
To show you the extent to which the lumber industry is affected by legislation I would remind the House that in Ontario until recent years there was nothing in the license granted to the lumberman requiring him to manufacture his lumber in the Dominion of Canada. He could put it into the rivers, float it down to the navigable waters and then tow it across to United 302
States centres. That was done in the Midland and Lake districts and the logs were towed to Bay City, Saginaw and Tonawan-da, there to be cut up into lumber, and Canada lost the benefit of the employment of that labour. This was the case all through the Georgian Bay and Midland districts of Ontario. Home after home was closed up, families had to move to the United States in order to obtain the wherewithal to live. The Hon. Mr. Whitney took the matter up and raised a very serious agitation, which forced the government of the day to place a clause in the contract requiring the lumberman to cut the lumber in the province of Ontario. Immediately, as if by magic, prosperity returned to the old towns along the Georgian Bay shores and through the Midland district of Ontario, wherever there was a lumbering centre, and our merchants, bankers, farmers, railways, every one in Canada has been more or less beneficially affected by that action in requiring these logs to be cut in Canada. I am satisfied that if a duty were placed upon lumber and timber coming from the United States into Canada it would have a similar effect throughout Canada. At the present time there is a great cry for Georgia pine in Canada. I know that a bridge was erected between Lindsay and Peterborough a few years ago by the Grand Trunk Railway of this imported pine. That bridge is to be replaced this year. Until recently our contractors and the constructors of bridges and those large works requiring heavy timber, thought that nothing could equal southern pine and it was brought in in immense quantities. The returns show that in some years $2,000,000 worth of this pine was brought in, but now they find that the British Columbia fir is superior in every respect and may be laid down more cheaply, other things being equal, than the southern pine is, that is if the southern pine is not sacrificed as it is to-day.
We are told that the imposition of the duty on lumber would be very detrimental to the interests of Manitoba and the Northwest. Sir, I cannot see it. Every part of Manitoba is convenient to some lumber camp. Hundreds of the boys from Manitoba farms go in the winter along the Rainy river, the Lake of the Woods district and all down that way and work in the camps. They are found all along the shores of Lake Winnipeg, Lake Winnipegosis and the lower Red Deer river. I know one gentleman alone who this winter employed 2,500 of these young men in the lumber camps in the northern part of Manitoba, and the eastern district of Saskatchewan. So, near the mountains, an enormous number of young men go to the mountain regions to work in the lumber camps during the winter months when they have nothing to do on the farms at home.
In that way it is a source of revenue, but this last winter the usual number of



men have not found employment, and in the coming year, I am informed on the best of authority by those engaged in the lumber business, that not only will wages be down but the employment of men will be very much reduced, almost entirely owing to the fact that we have no duty upon lumber coming from the United States or other lands into the Dominion of Canada. The trouble which has existed in Manitoba and the Northwest has not been due to the fact of a duty being on lumber . because there has been free trade in lumber. The trouble has been owing to a combine existing among the retailers which controls the prices and controls those engaged in the business. The argument that a duty on lumber would raise the price materially in these regions, I would think, if it is examined into, will be found not to hold good. But, even supposing that the duty were paid by the consumer-which is not in this case-it would not be a dollar a head for the farmers of Manitoba and the Northwest a year and they would, in the splendid home markets they would thereby have for their farm products in British Columbia, the Lake of the Woods and Rainy river country, lake Winnipeg and lake Winnipegosis and along the Red Derr river, make much more than any loss they would sustain by reason of the duty on lumber. I shall not weary the House with figures as it is not my intention at the present time to do more than point out in general terms the enormous quantity of wood material that is being imported into Canada. At the present time there is a great depression in the lumber business in the United States. People engaged in that industry, as in all businesses, require to pay interest on their bonds and investments and they are prepared to sacrifice their lumber for cost, land it here as cheaply as they may and get what they can for it rather than keep it and store it. I shall take the liberty of reading a little extract from Frank Leslie's Weekly which illus-tiates the possibility of selling* a certain portion of one's product at cost and still making considerable money, over what you might make by selling a smaller output at a higher figure. fit is a well known economic principle that it pays to keep mills -and men fully employed to the limit of capacity and time, even if part of the product has to be disposed of in foreign markets without profit or with slight sacrifice, rather than to curtail the facilities for production, and therefore reduce the earning capacity of the wage-workers. For, if every dollar so realized from foreign countries for surplus products, goes into the pockets of the wage-earners it increases the wealth of the country maintaining such policy. The Mr. SAM. following illustration taken from Josiah Strong's ' Expansion ' will serve to substantiate this statement: 'In a certain industry the profits are well established, according to the tonnage put through. If the run is 600 tons per day, the profits are $5,000 dollars per month. If the run is 900 tons per day, the profits are $20,000 per month. That is, by increasing the output fifty per cent, the profits are, in this instance, increased 300 per cent. If the extra 300 tons are sold at cost, it would leave the profits for the month $13,000; so that the extra 300 tons per day could actually be isold for $3,000 less .than cost and then the profits for the month would be twice as large as if only 600 tons had been run.
' This will sound to many very like the familiar old story of the peanut woman who, " always sold a little below cost and made her money by selling a great many." This statement, however, is capable of demonstration; 600 tons per day equals 18,000 tons per month; 900 tons per day equals 27,000 tons per month; market price of the product, $1.96 'per ton, leaving a profit of 28 cents per ton. At 900 toms per day the cost is reduced 'to $1.22, leaving a profit of 71 cents per ton. Now, 18,000 x 28 equals $5,010, the profits per month when only 600 tons are run per day; and 27,000 x 71 equals $19,980, the profits per month when 900 tons are run per day. If the entire increase of 9,000 toms is sold at cost, the 18,000 tons remaining would, at 74 cents per ton, make $13*320 instead of $5,010. So that these 9,000 tons might be sold for $3,000 less than cost and leave profits of $10,320 instead bf $5,040. Our laying hold of this principle was one of the reasons why we were able to enter European home markets, and it accounts for the fact that many articles of American manufacture can be bought cheaper in Europe than here.'
But, Sir, one of the worst features of the whole case is found in the fact that in the Southern States the pitch pine, which is exported to Canada in considerable quantity to-day, is all cut either by convict labour or coloured labour. Under the policy pursued by the government of Canada at the present time we are asking our men to live in this northern latitude to keep warm houses, purchase large quantities of fuel, dress warmly, educate their children -and the children of the Canadian lumbermen have just as good a right to an education as the children of any other class of people in the land-iu competition with people living in a southern climate where a yard of calico is their usual uniform both summer and winter. They have to compete with coloured and with convict labour. I notice in ' Everybody's Magazine ' for this month an article, not written along these lines, but intended to reform the abuses of the convict labour system in the southern and other States of the Union where convict labour is hired out or sold for whatever they can get per year for it, and that is the labour that is employed in the lumber (mills and manufacturing establishments. That is the class of labour that

our men in this northern latitude have to compete with under free trade in lumber. This article describes the brutality in connection with the treatment of these convicts, not alone by the jail authorities, but by the men to whom they are sold, and gives an account of the way in which a negro is flogged. Then it continues :
But the man has done wrong; he has committed a -fault.
Yes, from sunrise to noon he has wheeled fifty-seven loads of fresh brick; -the regulations of this hell on earth require -that in such a time he shall wheel six-ty loads. So, having thus transgressed, power and law and justice -as -administered in the state of Georgia exact from him this penalty until he screams and cries and sobs

and bleeds.
Further on the writer describes the meals.
For dinner they have each a piece of boiled salt pork, a piece of greasy corn bread. Although he is nearly famished, having worked all morning in the open air, the convict looks upon the food before him, and at -the recoi-leotion of -his breakfast has stomach revolts upon him and he turns sick and faints. But he gulps -down the corn bread -and, at last, turning the sa-lt -pork to the light -and -shredding it with his fingers, he -manages for sheer hunger's sake -to swallow a -li-ttle of it. The rest is begged by the hungry -man next to him. For supper he has boiled salt pork and a piece of corn bread. He learns that the state of Georgia does not f-urnAsh these viands' they are provided at the sole charge and cost of the company -to which -his slave labour has been sold.
That is in the issue of ' Everybody's Magazine' for the present month of June, and it goes on to describe how the State government has been taking action to improve the condition of these people. The free men in the Dominion of Canada, the 70,000 heads of families who are engaged in the lumber industry, have to compete, under free trade in lumber, with the coloured and convict labour of the United States of America.

I do not care whether you call it slave or convict labour; they have the worst system of slavery that they ever had at the present time. It is absolutely impossible to tell what lumber comes from a slave or convict mill and what comes from a free mill. At any rate wages are reduced by the competition of these convicts. Why are the prisons in Ontario going out of the convict labour business ? Simply because it brings convict labour into competition with free labour, it reduces the price of the commodity and in that way reduces wages just as it has done in the lumber business. Therefore, in the interest of the 70,000 odd free men, heads of families, men who want to bring their children up in respectability, in the interest of the men who have millions and millions of dollars invested in these mills up and down this country I would most respectfully impress upon the government the necessity of taking hold of this lumber question. At the present time there is scarcely a wheel turning in the lumber business in the province of Ontario. Banks are carrying these loads almost to their utmost limit. There is no market for lumber ; prices are down ; wages are down ; there is stagnation throughout the length and breadth of the province in the lumber business which calls for action by an up-to-date government. I trust that it will not be necessary that this matter should be brought to the attention of the House again, as it certainly will be if something is not done.
