The hon. member for Victoria (Mr. Sam. Hughes) said he did not wish to provoke any discussion. I have no doubt that would be the universal desire on the part of every gentleman who brings matters up ex parte before the Chair. But, even at the risk of transgressing the hon. gentleman's wishes, I would say a word or two to present, in a humble way, the views of those who do not agree with my hon. friend. There are those who would profit if any such duty were placed on lumber as my hon. friend has spoken of. I am glad, Mr. Speaker, that this matter has been brought before you by a private member and by one on the other side of the House; for I think I shall do no injury to these hon. gentlemen, I think I shall not be unjust to my hon. friend from St. Antoine. Montreal (Mr. Ames) if I say that if any hon. member on this side were to propose this increase in

duty It would be said by tbe opposition that he acted at the instance of the hon. member for Brandon (Mr. Sifton), the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Burrows) and others in order to increase the value of their limits. Therefore, even at the risk of not increasing the value of these limits, I will go further than that and ask if it be as hon. gentlemen opposite say that there is a vast fortune in the timber limits of the Northwest Territories and that the hon. member for Dauphin (Mr. Burrows), for example, and others have been made millionaires by the assets of the country being handed over to them, what is this proposed increase of duty for but to enhance the value of the assets which they are supposed to have received?
May I ask the hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles) a question? Are the limits to which he has referred worked? Are there thousands of men employed on these limits?

My answer, given without hesitation, is in the affirmative. I have no doubt that my hon. friend from St. Antoine will be able to explain )vhy these limits of my hon. friend from Dauphin and other hon. gentlemen engaged in the lumber business are so valuable as the hon. gentleman says and yet require this protection to make it worth while to operate them at all. The fact is that the hon. member for Dauphin and these other persons who are charged with being favourites of the government are operating largely the limits that they received and that is a fact that cannot be gainsaid.
My hon. friend (Mr. Sam. Hughes) has informed us as to the kinds of labour employed in tbe production of this lumber that is imported from the United States. He finds fault because negroes find employment in this work and because their product, the lumber from the south, is brought into Canada. I am sorry that the hon. member for West Kent (Mr. Clements) is not present, for I have no doubt that he would rise to defend the rights of the people of that race and that class, that they might not in this House have themselves classed with convicts or persons of that kind. And I cannot help

I must rise to a question of privilege. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Knowles) is putting words into my mouth that I did not utter. I was careful to point out the distinction between coloured labour and convict labour. ' Convict ' labour might include both coloured and white, but ' coloured ' refers to the negro.

My hon. friend's explanation is quite in harmony with what I was saying. The hon. gentleman in his remarks classed them together. Not once, but half a dozen times, he said that he objected to this lumber coming in as having been produced by convicts and negroes Mr. KNOWLES.
-or negroes and convicts, I do not know to which he gave second place. His making a bugbear of the fact that these imports are the product of the labour of negroes and convicts which he objects to, reminds me of the attitude of the hon. gentleman when the labour interests were being heard and those who were familiar with the facts were setting forth the views of organized labour. On that occasion the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sam. Hughes) was careful to say that he would have the Asiatics, such as the Hindus, come into this country rather than the galvanized Americans-not coloured Americans or convict Americans, but what he called ' galvanized' Americans, but still the industrious, hardworking. law-abiding, Anglo-Saxon Americans who, as they come among us, make just, as good citizens as any we have in this country.

I must again correct the hon. gentleman. X referred to the anarchists from the United States. I hope he does not associate with that class.
Mr. ICNOWIjES. I am not sure that X understood the hon. gentleman's question. Did he ask me if I associated him with anarchists ?
No. I asked the hon. gentleman (Mr. ICnowles) if he himself associated with anarchists; he seems ready to defend them.

I do not associate with anarchists. I am only saying that the hon. gentleman (Mr. Sam. Hughes) made the statement that he would rather have the Hindu come into this country than the ' galvanized ' Americans-that is the statement lie made. There are several remarks which might be made, speaking especially from the standpoint of the consumer of lumber in the Northwest in regard to the views of my hon. friend. He has said that those engaged in the lumber industry must have warm houses, for instance, which is something that those engaged in lumbering in Georgia do not need. But for one person engaged in cutting timber who must have a warm house we have five hundred or a thousand people who take up homesteads in the Northwest, who must first build houses and who must have those houses warm. On their behalf I protest against an agitation to increase the price to them of what is a prime necessity when they make their home in the Northwest. The very first requirement of homestead regulations is that a man shall have a house built. He must have a habitable house built; and it is well known that for a habitable house in that country you need a large quantity of lumber. l" remember that on one occasion the hon. member (Mr. Sam. Hughes) was careful to spread on the records of this House that he had a house on his large holding that he had built for

$SO. I think he will admit it would have cost him much more if $2 a thousand had been added to the price of the lumber used. And I think he will not say that he could build a house of a warm kind for any such sum.

Would the hon. gentleman point out how putting a duty on American lumber is going to increase the cost of lumber to the consumer? If he will break up the monopoly that he has in the west under free trade, he may be able to get the price of lumber reduced and this he can do by putting on a duty.

This is not to be a long discussion, so the hon. gentleman will not expect me to go into a consideration of the great economic question of how protection increases prices. 1 will not go into that question further than to give my own statement that protection does increase prices. I can only say that I will give my vote and voice on this basis. I believe that the people in my part of the country are convinced as I am that protection does enhance prices.
I may venture into the discussion so far as to ask the hon. member a question :	If
protection is not going to make a better market for his friends in the lumber business on whose behalf he speaks, what good will it do to them ? There will not be more lumber consumed ; there will not be a larger market; on the contrary there will be less consumed by reason of the increased price which I conted will be the result of the duty. One reason why we are always afraid of the men engaged in lumbering is that there is such danger that they will become combinsters, and I deliberately state that protection is the mother of trusts and combines. Tariffs breed trusts, and if there is one thing in which there should be no trust, that thing is lumber. For my part, I am against protection from start to finish, protection is to me an abomination. I support the Liberal party because of the two parties it is the one that favours the lower duties. But if a strong party decidedly devoted to free trade were to arise, I would be a supporter of that party, regarding its tariff policy. In this House, as representing my constituents, I believe I serve them best by supporting the party that goes the furthest in granting a low tariff. There can, therefore, in my humble opinion, be no reason for this increase of duty from the standpoint of the lumber industry, which is prosperous, whose men as a rule are wealthy men-you will find that in this city, where we are detained day after day and month after month, the wealthy men are those engaged in lumbering ; the prosperous people of the Northwest, those spoken of as millionaires by hon. members opposite are lumbermen ; the British Columbia lumbermen have been very prosperous for some years pafet. I
think the time is very ill-advised in asking for this increase. Our friends opposite deliberately placed themselves on record some years ago as being in favour of a duty of $2 a thousand on lumber which the lumbermen and their associations agitated for so strongly, but I am glad to say so unsuccessfully when they approached the present government which has maintained the low tariff.

MoLEAN (Queens, P.E.I.). I desire to bring to the attention of the House a matter which has already been partially discussed-the manner in which the Inland Revenue Department has conducted the business of inspecting tobacco factories. A few days ago, I brought to the attention of the House certain infractions of the regulations concerning the manufacture of tobacco. I wish to-night to take this matter up where I left off! before. I was prevented from proceeding on that occasion because it was contended by members on the government side of the House that I was not in order in the discussion, as this is a matter relating to the inland revenue while the item then before us is related to the customs.
As this is a matter of some importance I think it my duty to bring the whole correspondence to the attention of the House. There is a duty on imported tobacco of 10 cents per pound ; the excise duty is 25 cents per pound on imported ; on combination tobacco manufactured 5 cents per pound, and on Canadian tobacco 5 cents per pound. The case I refer to was the alleged infraction of the Inland Revenue Act and of the regulations thereunder, by the firm of T. B. and D. J. Riley, of the ciiy of Charlottetown. It was alleged that this firm had during the course of four years or longer- although they had two licenses, one for an imported leaf factory and one for a combination leaf factory-been in the habit of buying stamps for imported tobacco leaf alone and that they had been during all these four years committing frauds against the revenue of Canada by cutting stamps in two and putting half stamps upon the caddies of tobacco which they sold. It is clear that if a person commits this offence he is guilty of a criminal act, and if such an infraction of the law be drawn to the ntten-tion of the officers of the Crown it is the duty of the inland revenue officers to take such proceedings as the law provides to punish the guilty parties. It is laid down ' in the Criminal Code, section 479 :

The evidence produced to the officers of the department showed clearly and distinctly that such an Infraction of the law as would come within section 479 of the Criminal Code was committed, and yet the inland revenue authorities condoned the offence. They condoned it by allowing the junior member of this firm to pay $200 as a condonation of the offence which they had committed against the Inland Revenue Act and also against the Criminal Code, and the Department of Inland Revenue, accepted that $200 in full requital of the offence which these men committed. In order to make this matter more clear I will read the regulations governing the manner In which officers of the Inland Revenue Department are required to conduct themselves in regard to the manufacture of tobacco and the Inspection of the manufactories. Section II provides:
The officer in charge of each tobacco or cigar manufactory shall keep a record of the weight of all packages of raw leaf or other raw material received by the .manufacturers. The entry shall be .made in a book provided by the department focr that purpose.

Then it goes on to show in sectiou 36 of the regulations what the duties of the officers are. It is provided that every tobacco manufactory in this country must have an officer in charge who shall look after it and see that all the provisions of the Inland Revenue Act and the regulations made under it by the Governor in Council have been complied with. Section 36 of the regulations provide :
lit is the duty of every officer in charge of any (tobacco or cigar manufactory to see that no greater quantity of tobacco or cigars is contained in the packages to which the stamps are attached than the stamp is intended to cover and all the packages must in all cases be full, i.e., a ten pound stamp must not be placed on /a package capable of holding from fifteen to twenty pounds even if the package only contains ten pounds of tobacco. Should any package containing tobacco or cigars at any time be discovered with stamps thereon for less than the package contains, it is the duty of every officer to detain such packages as forfeited and report the circumstances to this department through the collector of the division.
Now, the meaning of these regulations and of the law is that the officers shall see that the packages contain the proper

quantity of tobacco and shall also see that the proper stamps shall be placed on those packages. In this case a complaint was made to the collector of Inland revenue in the city of Charlottetown. As was stated here on the 26th of May, in the discussion which then took place, and in the letters which were then read, the collector of inland revenue in the city of Charlottetown did not give the matter any consideration, or did not give it sufficient consideration, and the parties who are aggrieved in this matter, namely, the Hickey & Nicholson Tobacco Company, Limited, who are tobacco manufacturers in the city of Charlottetown. complain that they are not receiving justice at the hands of the officers of the Inland Revenue Department. After they had informed them that to their own knowledge many breaches of these regulations had been committed, they were compelled to go to the collector of customs of Charlottetown, Mr. W. B. Robertson. Mr. Robertson found that an infraction of the law had been committed by the firm of T. B. & D. J. Riley. He found the evidence of the breach of the lawr at the store of Mr. W. A. Poole, Lower Montague, in King's County. Mr. Robertson reported the fact to the commissioner of customs in the city of Ottawa, and asked him if he would have his permission to investigate the matter. The commissioner gave his permission, and Mr. Robertson then investigated the matter and reported to the commissioner of customs in Ottawa. He also sent the declarations of Mr. Donald Nicholson and of Mr. Harnett, which set out a large number of infractions of the law which had been committed, or which had been alleged to have been committed by this firm of T. B. & D. J. Riley-something like fifteen or sixteen. Notwithstanding this fact and the fact that Mr. Harnett had reported the matter to the officers of the Inland Revenue Department, he received no satisfaction from them, and he was compelled to go to the collector of customs, who was not the proper officer to report the matter to ; but when the collector of customs received the sanction of the commissioner of customs to investigate, and did investigate, and found that these allegations were worthy of investigation, and so reported to his department, the commissioner of customs, after the declarations of Mr. Nicholson and Mr. Harnett had come to Ottawa, reported to Mr. Gerald, the deputy Minister of Inland Revenue, and Mr. Gerald sent one of his officers, Mr. Burke, who has supervision lof the factories in the maritime provinces, to Charlottetown. He went there and found no infraction of the law. The next man sent there was Mr. Fitzgerald, who did not report that any infraction of the law had been committed. Still, these gentlemen, who knew that an infraction of the law had
been committed, persisted in their efforts to obtain justice at the hands of the government, particularly the Inland Revenue Department, and they requested through the collector of customs at Charlottetown that another investigation be made. The Inland Revenue Department then sent Mr. Caven, of Montreal, an officer of the Inland Revenue Department, to the city of Charlottetown to see if there was any truth in the reports which had been declared by Mr. Nicholson and Mr. Harnett with reference to these alleged infractions of the law. Before Mr. Caven went down, I presume that Messrs. Riley found out that an investigation was to take place, one perhaps more severe than the two previous ones, and they saw fit to send up to the department the sum of $200. This is the letter which Mr. D. J. Riley, the junior member of that firm, sent to the department at Ottawa with the $200 :
I hereby abandon the sum of $200, deposited with Mr. S. C. Nash, collector of inland revenue, Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island. This abandonment is made under section 136 of the Inland Revenue Act.
That letter is dated Charlottetown, October 10, 1907. Before this document was signed by D. J. Riley, and before the money was paid to Mr. Nash, it was positively declared, under the Act relating to extra judicial oaths, before Mr. Robertson, the collector of customs in Charlottetown, that these men had committed not only an infraction of the Inland Revenue Act in not having placed stamps upon some of the tobacco they sold, but also an infraction of the Criminal Code, in having mutilated the stamp, that offence coming under section 479 for which they were liable to imprisonment for 14 years in the penitentiarv. He asked if I thought the department would be willing to let matters go if he gave up his license, that for some time they had been losing money in bad debts and as all this trouble would come on his unole, Mr. T. B. Riley, he, D. J. Riley, would be willing to go away from the business. He asked me if I would call and see Mr. T. B. Riley who was sick and unable to come out. I called and saw him. He showed me two drafts for leaf which he had not accepted, for, if the department were going to seize his factory and sell him out he would countermand the leaf order. I told him that the department could impose a fine for any offences D. J. Rilev -had been guilty of. I have no doubt that D. J. Riley has been guilty of infractions of the Act, but so long had elapsed between the time of the tobacco being placed upon the market and my visit that Riley was able to go around the country and get any stock that remained upon the merchants' hands.
I vasated Riley's factory -and asked him if he would take his -ledger and check off the items wa-th stock -book No. 2. He said he kept no ledger

He said he kept uo ledger.
-day book or order.
He kept no ledger, day blook or order book, and here is the law laid down distinctly, not only in the Act but in the regulations as well, that every manufacturer of tobacco must keep a full and particular account of all tobacco that he uses and all stock which he has in his factory. Notwithstanding this fact the Department of Inland Revenue lets rest that point and accept in condonation of all the offences which these men have committed. I
I visited Riley's factory and asked him i he would take his ledger and check off th< items with stock book No. 2. He said he kep no ledger, day book or letter book. All hii sales were cash or draft and he -relied so-leb on stock book No. 2. I then asked him t< snow me entries for one or two items whidl were in stock book No. 2, -but no trace of then appeared in either of his books. On the after noon of the day this took -place I visited -Sourii and called upon Messrs. Mathew & McLear and Stern Brothers. They gave me a memo of -the dates, packages and pounds of tobacec bought from Riley. Messrs. Stern Brothers told me that they bought from Riley on open account and that Riley would draw upon them Mr. A. A. McLEAN.
Here is a statement made to the Department of Inland Revenue in Ottawa, but still no action was taken upon it. Notwithstanding the fact that it was reported to the department that these men had committed these infractions of the law and had had time through the blundering of theii? own officers to go around and take back the tobacco no action had been taken by the department.
. tDhe three caddies referred to by Mr. Moore -in store of Mathew & McLean -were -likely covered by half stomps and Mr. Moore now sees he was in error in not taking -the tobacco to the excise office in Charlottetown.
I am of the opinion that no further trouble will be caused by Riley as, acting upon instructions from Inspector Burke, Mr. Nash or Mr. Moore see that all -the stamps are properly affixed to caddies.
Was it not the duty of some officer to to see that these stamps were affixed to the caddies? How is the public to be guarded ^ against infractions of the law if the officials appointed to see that the law is enforced do not perform that duty?
On my return -to Montreal I consulted with Mr. Lawlor, who advised me that in the absence of any proof other than Riley's admission i-t would be well to write Collector Nash and ask that Riley deposit the sum of $200 aB a penalty under section 36 of the Inland Revenue Act. This I did and attach hereto abandonment for amount stated, Mr. Lawlo-r is

absent on a trip of inspection and for this reason I am sending my report direct to you.
I remain, sir,
Tour obedient servant,
(Sgd.) W. CAVEN, Deputy Collector.
To the Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue,
Ottawa.
I have no doubt that Mr. Caven did his duty to the best of his ability, that he is a man who knows how to do his duty, but that he was duped by these men in this way, that he agreed to accept, or to report to the department that they should accept, $200 in condonation of these previous offences against the law.
They refer in this abandonment to section 136 of the law, and they say, in effect : This department says that if a manufacturer of tobacco buys $1,000 or $2,000 or $3,000 or $4,000 or $10,000 worth of stamps, cuts them in two and cheats and - defrauds the public in this way, he can abandon $200 and cheat the revenue out of $60,000 or $70,000 or $80,000 or $100,000. Is that the law? It is not the law, it is not the meaning of the law. Under the section referred to the government had no right to accept it at all. What is the meaning of this section? It reads :
If any article or thing is voluntarily given up or abandoned by the owner to any collector or superior officer as forfeited under this Act, or if any sum of money is voluntarily paid to any such collector or officer as the amount of a penalty under this Act, such article or thing may be dealt with as if lawfully condemned and such sum of money as if lawfully recovered.
Supposing the government did their duty strictly according to the letter of the law, they could have confiscated his factory. Suppose it had been shown that Riley had committed one infraction of the law, suppose that he had not (under the provision of the law), used the proper die to cancel the stamp, which he had bought from the government, perhaps he could in the case of one infraction abandon the sum of $200. But where there were many infractions, where It was known to the government that for a period of at least three or four years these infractions of the law had been committed by these men, that seventeen or eighteen infractions had been brought home to them, was it then the duty of the gov-i eminent to accept $200 as full satisfaction for all these offences? I do not think it was. I do not think the government were justified, or that the public will say that the government did right in accepting this sum of $200. I think that when men commit many infractions of the law as these men had done, proceedings should have been taken by the Department of Inland Revenue to punish them. They were just as guilty under the law as if they had forged my name or that of the Minister of
Inland Revenue, the same penalty would apply to a forgery as to the mutilation of a stamp. Why then, were these men not punished? I think I can tell you, because the senior member of this firm was the vicepresident of the Liberal association of the county of Queens, that is why the name of T. B. Riley was left out of the proceedings which were taken by the officers of the Inland Revenue Department. That is the reason why, notwithstanding the fact that the government had issued a license to T. B. Riley, they accepted the abandonment of $200 from his partner D. J. Riley. That is the reason, there is no other reason. Politics entered into all these proceedings, even into matters which concerned the condonation of offences which are punishable by imprisonment for fourteen years in the penitentiary.
Notwithstanding that these men were guilty of these infractions of the law, notwithstanding the fact that the deputy Minister of Inland Revenue was acquainted with the circumstances of the case, he allows the matter to go, not a word said, but accepting this paltry sum of $200 in satisfaction. That is not the way it would have been if Hickey, Nicholson Co., Limited, had committed an infraction of the law, for they happen to be on the other side of politics. These men had been greatly handicapped by the way the government had allowed the Rileys to do their business for years, paying only half the amount of duty, or, in many cases, no duties at all, on the tobacco they manufactured. This is one of the most glaring cases that has ever been known. I do not think the time has elapsed in which action can be taken against these men who committed this offence against the government.	-
The government took this cheque. The cheque was sent to the assistant commissioner of customs, and, in a letter dated January 10, 1908, addressed to Mr. Gerald by Mr. Farrow, he said :
I have the honour to acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 7th instant inclosing departmental cheque No. 1859 in favour of the commissioner for the sum of $50 covering an award made for information furnished by our collector of customs at Charlottetown respecting the irregular stamping of packages of tobacco by a manufacturer in Charlottetown.
The cheque has this day been forwarded to the collector of customs ait Charlottetown and he has been requeued to send proper receipts to this department for transmission to yon.
Why did the Minister of Inland Revenue accept this cheque ? There were many_ infractions of the law, besides the criminal one to which I referred, the highest penalty for which would be $500 and the lowest $100 ? Eighteen cases were presented to him which would amount to something like $9,000, and still he allows these men off for

$200. When I am through, I hope the minister will answer me and state why he allowed these infractions of the law of which he is the especial administrator, and also this offence against the criminal law to go unpunished except for this paltry $200. A good deal of correspondence took place with regard to payment. It seems that the sum of $50 was due to somebody for giving information against these people. It was offered to Mr. Robertson, but he did not think he was entitled to it. Evidently it was thought that Mr. Harnett, of the Hickey-Nicholson Co., Ltd., who had given the information, was entitled to it. Mr. Gerald wrote to Mr. Robertson requesting that the $50 be paid over to Mr. Harnett, but Mr. Harnett informed Mr. Robertson that he would not accept any sum of money from the government of Canada for giving the information. And he informs me that he does not consider the punishment accorded to these men was sufficient for the serious offences they had committed. He informed the department through Mr. Robertson, the collector of customs in Charlottetown, that he would have nothing to do with the $50 and also informed him that he thought that, in giving this information against these men, he was only doing his duty to himself and to the public as a citizen of Canada, that he desired his action to be gratis and not for remuneration, and also that the punishment meted out to these men was not sufficient. The letter that Mr. Robertson wrote on this subject is set out in the return laid on the table. It is not necessary for me to read it. In my opinion, this case from first to last is a most glaring-injustice committed against the firm of Hickey-Nicholson, of Charlottetown, tobacco manufacturers, who were competing with the Rileys and that the punishment meted out to these offenders was not at all commensurate with the crimes they had committed.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
It is much to be regretted that my hon. friend (A. A. McLean) did not send me an intimation that he proposed bringing up this matter this evening. While this pertains to the Inland Revenue Department, the matter is one which arose some six months ago, it is one concerning which there was a considerable correspondence, and all the facts are not at this moment very clear in my recollection. My hon. friend read most of the correspondence the other eveniug when the House was in Supply. I assume that he was more concerned then-and is more concerned now- in placing the facts before the public of Prince Edward Island for political purposes than in any other phase of the question. For there is politics in this, as the two manufactures of tobacco in Charlottetown are politicians, one on one side and the other on the other side. I believe that this man Mr. A. A. McLEAN.
Riley, guilty of contravention of the Inland Revenue Act, is not of the same political persuasion as my hon. friend.
Now, this is not a matter to take up very much time. Mr. Riley is a tobacco manufacturer. It was discovered-I think the information first came from a rival manufacturer-by an inland revenue officer that the tobacco manufactured by Riley Bros, was not sufficiently stamped. The officer of the Inland Revenue Department named Moore, made an investigation, and found in some of the country stores caddies of tobacco that were insufficiently stamped- half the quantity of stamps being placed on these caddies. This officer of the Inland Revenue Department, Moore, certainly failed in the discharge of his duty right at that point. When he found the tobacco insufficiently stamped, he went away leaving the tobacco in the possession of the parties who owned it, requesting the parties, I believe, to keep it in a safe place or not to dispose of it, and he would return. Now, that tobacco was never seen again. It had been returned to another Riley who was a retail dealer-there are two firms of Riley, one manufacturers and the other storekeepers. Mr. Burke, the inspector from St. John, N. B., went there to investigate the case under instructions from the deputy Minister of Inland Revenue. Mr. Haven also was sent and his report has been read by my hon. friend. Mr. Caven found that three, or four, or probably, half a dozen caddies of tobacco had been sent out with insufficient inland revenue stamps upon them. These caddies having disappeared, it was absolutely impossible to prove anything against Riley the manufacturer. Mr. Caven, the deputy collector from Montreal who was sent down by Mr. Lawlor, our inspector, reports as follows :
I have no doubt but that D. J. Riiley has been guilty of infractions of the Aot, but so long had elapsed between the time of the tobacco being placed upon the market and my visit that Riley was able to go round the country and get any stock that remained upon the merchants' .hands.
That is precisely what happened.
The three caddies referred to by Mr. Moore in store of Matthew & McLean were likely covered by half stamp and Mr. Moore now sees that he was in error in not taking the tobacco to the excise office in Charlottetown.
The evidence of the guilt of Riley the manufacturer had disappeared. Mr. Caven said :
On my return to Montreal I consulted with Mr. Lawlor

Our head inspector and a very excellent official.
-who advised me -that in the absence of any proof other than Riley's admission it would be well to write Collector Nash and ask that Riley deposit the sum of - $200 as a penalty under section 136 of Inland Revenue Aot.

'Mr. A. A. McLEAN. Could the hon. gentleman not get evidence from Mr Harnett and also from Mr. Moore? They had the evidence of Mr. Harnett, Mr. Moore, Mr. Nicholson, Mr. Burke and 'Matthew and McLean.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: Their evidence would not have been sufficient.
You had the evidence of Mr. Harnett before this letter was written and signed by Mr. Robertson, the collector of customs at Charlottetown.
There was the evidence of eighteen men that you could have got.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: These are the facts of the case. The goods had disappeared and if we had undertaken a prosecution against Riley it would have failed as we rwere advised. He was asked to deposit $200 and that amount he forfeited.
Did you not want that advice ?

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext:
I cannot say. The swhole matter transpired before I had any knowledge of the events at all ; so that I cannot say that I wanted advice one way or the other. The $200 were accepted and further proceedings were dropped. These are the whole facts of the case. I admit frankly that the officers of the Inland Revenue Department at Charlottetown did not do their duty. When they found that there was a contravention of the law, or an infringement of the Inland Revenue Act, or a fraud on the part of Mr. Riley, they ought to have taken possession of the goods and obtained the evidence that would have convicted him of fraud. They did not do so. In several other cases of the same kind where there have been infractions of the Inland Revenue law and where it has been impossible to convict the party guilty of these infractions, deposits have been received and they have been forfeited to the department under the provisions of the Inland Revenue Act. There is a lot of correspondence between the customs officials and the Inland Revenue officials, but, boiled down, the simple explanation is as I have stated. There was no violation, whatever, of the Customs Act. There was no fraud upon the customs. The fraud was upon the Inland Revenue. We have no reason to know to what extent, but we have been assured that these frauds were very limited indeed. We have no positive information that they involved more than three or four caddies. There may have been more but it would have been impossible to have continued frauds of that kind for any length of time. My officers advised me that *they do not think the frauds were very extensive. In so far as I am advised, I think the ends of justice have been served by fining this manufacturer $200. My hon.
friend who raised this question cannot say that the frauds were long continued or that they amounted to very much. If we had had sufficient evidence of course, we might have seized or confiscated the manufacturer's factory, but we did not think, with the very poor evidence we had, that it would be wise to do so. We pursued this course and we think we pursued the right one.

I will not attempt to take up very much of the time of the House on this question as I have not gone into it so fully as my hon. friend (Mr. A. A. McLean), but after looking over the evidence that my hon. friend brought before the House the other evening and his statement of the case to-day I think that the hon. Minister of Inland Revenue (Mr. Templeman) treats the matter in a very light and easy fashion. As in many other cases which have been brought before the House and the country, they are trying to cover up the abuses in the different departments of the government which have occurred possibly through the fault of their own officials. They are not, in going after a situation of this kind, getting down to the root of the matter, but they are approaching it from the point of view of protecting their os'n political friends as my hon. friend from Queens has pointed out. To my mind this case shows an obvious abuse, an evasion of the law and the Department of Inland Revenue have not gone after it in a proper manner to discover these people and find out how many infringements of the Act have taken place. The Minister of Inland Revenue says to my hon. friend : You did not say there were a great many infractions of the law.
I find in the evidence of Mr. Harnett, taken by the collector of customs, that these cases ran from May, 1906, to August, 1907. I do not think that the department used the means at their disposal to find out how many infractions of the law there were. I believe' that while the minister treats it in a very light manner there were thousands upon thousands of dollars taken out of the revenue of this country and put into the pockets of these manufacturers of Charlottetown. and that not only were they stealing the money of the country, but they were robbing other people of the trade to which they were fairly entitled by selling their tobacco at a cheaper rate than the manufacturers who were complying with the law could sell it at and compete against them at a profit. I have heard it stated by parties who have figured it up that these transactions extended over four years and ran into from $40,00 to $60,000, of which amount the revenue of the country was defrauded. You can easily understand that when it amounts to $5 a caddy it will not take long to run up to $60,000. The minister acknowledges

that he is not very familiar with the situation. I can very readily understand from his remarks that he was not familiar with it I have only had an opportunity of reading over the papers during the last hour and 1 can see that there is some conclusive evidence in the documents that there was an absolute case of wrong-doing. Prom the evidence produced it seems clear that there was at least collusion with those in high places, and that the government of the country has condoned this wrong-doing and shielded the perpetrators, tinder section 479 of the Criminal Code it is the duty of the officials of the Inland Revenue Department to take criminal proceedings against those who mutilate or fraudulently use Inland Revenue stamps. It was shown that, in a number of instances, these parties, T. B. and D. J. Riley, did mutilate these stamps that they cut them in two and put half of one on a caddy instead of the regulation stamp. The evidence showed this fraud to have been committed and the government condoned this -wrong by the acceptance of a $200 fine when they had the evidence in their hands that fraud had been committed. The minister has tried to make this House believe that there was no evidence to prove these parties guilty. There were affidavits before this letter from Mr. Caven came to hand of a number of reputable merchants of Prince Edward Island and there were fifteen or eighteen cases sworn to by Mr. Harnett before the commissioner of customs. Surely this was sufficient evidence to prove that these people had been guilty of a fraudulent act under the Criminal Code. Yet the minister thinks there was nothing proved. It seems to me that the business of the Inland Revenue Department, in the different parts of the Dominion, must be carried on very carelessly. Section 11 of the regulations regarding the manufacture of tobacco requires the officials to keep recordiS, ledgers and other accounts of the amount of leaf received and of the amount that is used in the manufacture of tobacco. Section 44 of these regulations requires that the manufacturer shall also keep books and it is provided that the books of the officers of the department and the manufacturer shall correspond. There must have been an obvious neglect of duty on the part of the minister's officers to enable these people to get up and testify that they kept no books and could show no record. Tlie regulations require that an officer of the Inland Revenue Department shall take account of all the leaf that is in the possession of the manufacturer and that he shall keep it under lock and key.

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: There is no doubt at all that the manufacturing firm of Rileys kept books according to the requirements of the department. It is the other firm of Rileys, local traders, the father or brother of the manufacturer, who it is said kept no books.
That is not correct. It is the firm of T. B. & D. J. Riley who kept no books. As we understand

speakerposition: Minister of Mines; Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: I do not know what is understood, but I say that the manufacturing firm of Rileys kept all the books and made all the entries required by the department.

Mr. Caven writes :
I visited Riley's factory and asked him if he would take ihis ledger and cheek off the items with his stock book Jjo. 2. He said he kept no ledger, day book or order book, all his sales were cash or draft and he relied wholly on stock book No. 2.
He was asked to produce his books and he said he kept no books and, therefore, according to the evidence of Mr. Caven he did not comply with the law. The Department of Inland Revenue should not have dealt with one of the Rileys individually and accepted a fine of $200 from him, but they should have punished the firm of T. B. & D. J. Riley who were the offenders. The statement of the minister that there was no evidence to prosecute these men under the criminal code is not borne out by the facts which he had before him, but which he acknowledges he did not consider very carefully. On August 5, 1907, Mr. Nash, collector of inland revenue, wrote to the Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue as follows :
Inland Revenue Division No. 1, Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island,
August 5, 1907.
W. J. Gerald, Esq.,
Deputy Minister of Inland Revenue, Ottawa.
Sir,-I have the honour to state that rumours of tobacco being sold * out of packages ' have reached this office. Kings county seems to be the habitat. I have requested Inspector Burke to come over sooner than usual, although he is due some time this month when we might make some, arrangements to make seizures. In the meantime I have sent Officer Moore to one or two places to investigate and have also instructed him on his collecting tours to visit shops where tobacco is sold and seize in every case illiotly exposed tobacco. I have made requisition to-day for forms.
Question-'Is it necessary to remove tobacco seized? I mean to take possession.
I am your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) SAMUEL C. NASH,
Collector Inland Revenue.
This is the answer :
Ottawa, August 8, 1907.
S. C. Nash, Esq.,
Collector of Inland Revenue, Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island.
Sir,-I am in receipt of your communication of the 5th instant respecting the rumoured sale of unstamped tobacco within your division and requesting to be advised as to the necessity for taking possession of such tobacco in case of seizure
In reply thereto I beg to state that if tobacco is so seized it becomes the property of

the Crown and if the faots warrant its seizure they certainly necessitate taking possession of the goods seized.
In connection of the matter of seizure of tobacco, out of stamped packages, great care should be used by our officials to endeavour to ascertain if it is a case of fraud or of simple ignorance of the law. While it is true that the latter is no justification for the *wrong-doing it is a factor that should have some weight with our officials.
In any case whether tobacco is so found or not our officer should explain to dealers visited the provisions of the law respecting the sale of tobacco and, if these dealers have not been supplied with circular G-155, a copy thereof should be delivered to each person visited and should be mailed to persons who are not so personally called upon.
I remain, sir,
Your obedient servant
Deputy Minister.
The firm of Hickey & Nicholson were of course subject to unfair competition on account of this defrauding of the revenue by a rival firm and they suspected the officers of the department were not moving fast enough, and so "on August 9 this letter was written :
Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, August 9, 1907.
W. B. Robertson, Esq.,
Collector of Customs.
Sir,-Our Mr. Harnett has drawn my attention to gross violations.of the Excise and Customs Act and I have reported the same to other officers some time ago, but up to the present no action has been taken or likely to. I therefore report same to you now and demand that you take immediate action and our Mr. Harnett will accompany yon to the identical goods.
Yours respectfully,
(Sgd.) HENRY NICHOLSON TOBACCO
COMPANY, Limited.

Mr. Robertson, in pursuance of the information which he had received, went to Lower Montague and discovered that irregularities in some of the tobacco of T. B. & D. J. Riley bad been perpetrated, and fraud committed against the people and government of this country. He reported it to the Commissioner of Customs. Would not that be proof enough to the Minister of Inland Revenue that fraud was being perpetrated when he had it on his own officer's report? The next letter is written on the 10th of August and it is as follows:
Department of Customs, port of Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island,
August 10, 1907.
Sir,-I beg to report that acting on the inclosed letter from the Hickey & Nicholson Company, Limited, I drove to Lower Montague, and called on the firm of W. A. Poole & Company, and while they have no tobacco on hand at the present moment irregularly stamped, I gleaned enough evidence from Mr. George Poole, a member of the firm, to satisfy me that things are not straight so far as the
stamping of the .tobacco sent out by the firm of T. B. & D. J. Riley, of this city, are concerned, and I am confident that the circumstances are such as would justify a searching investigation and trust that all may meet with your honourable approval.
I have the honour to he, sir.
Your obedient servant,
(Sgd.) W. B. ROBERTSON.
The Commissioner of Customs on August 7 wrote to the collector of customs at Charlottetown, P.E.I., as follows :
August 7.
To the Collector of Customs,
Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island.
Sir,-1 have the honour to 'acknowledge the receipt of your letter of the 10th instant, respecting the irregular stamping of tobacco at your port. You may inquire into and report such irregularities as you find in the tobacco sent out by T. B. and D. J. Riley.
I have the honour to be, sir,
Your obedient servant,
Commissioner of Customs.
Mr. Robertson took the trouble to Investigate and the result is contained in a report marked schedule A, and declaration A and declaration B ; and I want the minister, who apparently is not familiar with the correspondence, to listen to the declarations signed by the commissioner of Customs, who was authorized by the deputy minister of Customs to make the investigation. The first is as follows :
I, Donald Nicholson, of Charlottetown, a member of the Hickey & Nicholson Tobacco Company, Limited, do hereby declare that during the early spring I called officer Theop. Moore's attention to the fact that insufficiently stamped tobacco was sold throughout the country, and he promised me to keep a sharp lookout for it.
About the last of July, on his return from Souris, I inquired if he had discovered any such tobacco, and he replied that ' he saw mole than he wanted to see.' Viz., 3 caddies of Rilev tobacco at Messrs. Mathew & McLeans' and had ordered the clerk to lay them aside as he might require them. He then accompanied me to Mr. Nash and we fully discussed the matter and Mr. Nash agreed to send for the inspector.
On August 7 our salesman, Mr. Harnett, telephoned me from Georgetown that Messrs. W. A. Poole & Company, Lower Montague, had such tobacco on hand and suggested that I see the Inland Revenue officer at once, and I informed Mr. Moore of it on that date. Mr. Harnett returned home on the 8th, and on the 9th he and I called on Mr. Nash urging that they take immediate action and offering to drive the officer to where it was sold, hut Mr. Moore being out of town and Mr Nash, who treated the matter somewhat lightly, was too busy, so we called on the collector of customs and demanded that he take immediate action. On Mr. Harnett's agreeing to accompany him they left on the morning of the 10th for Lower Montague.
[Inspector Burke arrived here on the 13th and on the 14th sent for me, after a short interview we parted, and he, I am told, left

for home on the 15th, and so far we have not heard if anything has been done.
(Sgd.) DONALD NICHOLSON,
President pf Company.
Signed and declared before me at Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island, this 22nd day of August, A.D. 1907.
(Sgd.) W. B. ROBERTSON, Collector.
I would like to know why this man Moore was not called to give evidence. He saw more than he wanted to see, and I presume that the department knew more than they wanted to make public. The Mr. Burke who is referred to in this declaration was the inspector for the maritime provinces. The next declaration that I would call to the attention of the hon. Minister is declaration B which is made by Mr. Harnett :
I, Evelyn B. Harnett, a member of the firm of Hickey and Nicholson Tobacco Company, Limited, acting as travelling salesman for the Lower provinces do hereby solemnly affirm that I examined tobacco sent out by the firm of Messrs. T. B. and D. J. Riley of Charlottetown on the dates and at the places mem-tioned below and found it insufficiently stamped and noted same in my memorandum hook, viz.:
There are eases here running from August, 1906, to August, 1907, during which this abuse was going on. In the early spring of 1907 Mr. Nicholson, of the firm of Hickey & Nicholson, drew this to the attention of the officers of the department; but no action was taken upon it until August, 1907. There are here some twenty or twenty-five cases of ponclusive evidence that the Department of Inland Revenue was being defrauded. Mr. Harnett, after going over a number of these cases, says :
About May 15, last I met Mr. Moore, of the Inland Revenue Department at our factory and in the presence of Mr. D. Nicholson informed him that I had seen insufficiently stamped tobacco and urged them to look into the matter.
On August 7 I visited Lower Montague and found at the store pf Messrs. W. A. Poole & Company, 5 caddies of Riley's tobacco, 1 full stamped, 3 half stamped and one without stamps and I reported this to Mr. Nicholson by telephone from Georgetown and suggested that he see the inland revenue officer at once, I returned to Charlottetown on the evening of the 8th instant, and on the 9th I called on Mr. Nash to discuss the matter, and as he treated it so lightly, I in company with Mr. Nicholson called on the collector of customs and I demanded that he give it immediate attention, and I volunteered to show where it was exposed for sale. On the 10th the collector and I drove to Lower Montague and called on Messrs. W. A. Poole & Company and was told that George Riley, of Charlottetown, a brother to T. W. Riley and father to D. J. Riley, drove to their store on the 8th of August and of his own free will and without being requested by W. A. Poole took possession and carried away two caddies without stamps, promising to return fresh stock instead, and left one caddie

with half stamps on partly used on the shelf.
On the 9th Mr. Moore who was out collecting samples of food called at Messrs. Poole's store and inquired if Mr. Riley had been there lately, and when told he was there on the 8th he looked over the stock of tobacco on hand. One caddie with stamps and one with half stamps partly used on the shelf, which was opened in the end, he, Mr. Moore, took the hatchet and opened it on the side, remarking that was the proper way to open it, and after the collector held a conversation with Mr. Poole, one of the firm, we returned to town.
On the evening of the 13th I, in company with Robert W. D. M. Rattery, foreman of our factory, called on Inspector Burke at the Queen's Hotel, and after discussing the matter Mr. Burke informed us that he had no idea of the seriousness of the offence and promised to see Mr. Nicholson in the morning. Mr. Burke returned home on the morning of the 15th and so far as I am aware nothing has been done.

McLean), it is clear that the officers of the department had in their hands evidence of irregularities to justify them in taking very stringent measures to suppress the wrong, which was not only a wrong against the country in depriving it of its revenues, but a wrong against people who were manufacturing tobacco in the same city, and who were compelled to sell at reduced rates and make no profit, while these people were profiting at the expense of the country. Mr. Harnett, who gave the information, was certainly justified in refusing what might almost be said to have been a bribe to hush up the matter. He feels very much humiliated that his four colleagues are increased from $1,000 to $1,800 while his salary is not increased. I may say that Mr. Bourinot is such a terror to smugglers along our coast that there is scarcely any smuggling done, and, if he is confined to what he can collect from seizures on account of smuggling, what he receives will amount to very little. But what he feels most keenly is not being kept on the same plane as his colleagues of this service.

The Minister of Customs (Mr. Paterson) said that he expected to get this money in a few minutes and to be able to distribute it. Am I to understand that as soon as the item is passed he can use the money ? He must wait for a Supply Bill, must he not ? He said the other day that as soon as he got the vote passed he would issue the cheques.

Mr. Leinieux, inspector at Montreal, receives for nine months a salary of $1,687.50 and for board and lodging $222.50. There are vouchers supplied for the latter payment, I presume? The minister says there are vouchers for all the items of expenditure.
I understand so.
Cabs, busses and ferries, $45.75 ; fares, $67.83 ; leather bag, $20. What kind of a bag would that be and why was it supplied to this officer?
I suppose it was a travelling bag for his books and papers.

Yes; the accountant tells me there is a voucher for everything.
There is an item, pullmans and porters, $34.25. Does he get a voucher from a porter when he tips him? Mr. McLennan.
No.

Then the minister must withdraw a portion of the statement that he made that there is a voucher for everything. We find these officers throwing out the people's money in pullmans and tips to porters. Hundreds of dollars are expended in this way. The minister says there are vouchers and now he admits there are no vouchers for these expenditures.
You must take things in the broad and not get down to quibbles.

I find that Mr. Jones, inspector, received a salary of $1,500 for nine months; that would, I presume, be $2,000 for the year. He received for board and lodging, $600; cabs and cartage, $83.80; livery, $25.50; pullman and porters, $53.45; telephone rent, $27.40; petty expenses, $16.85, making $2,351. There is a large amount going out for travelling expenses, pullmans, tips to porters. The minister said that there was a voucher for every item and now he admits there are np vouchers for a portion of these expenses. I would like to see the vouchers for the petty expenditures.

We do not get vouchers for tips. When you ask the question I can quite understand that there are vouchers for these items and that the Auditor General is satisfied when he sees that there are some charges for tips and pullmans. Inspector McMichael has to come down here and in order to save time we ask him to come down by night. We pay his pullman berth.
If his account is certified by one of the officers of the department the Auditor will pay it without vouchers?
Yes.
