The vouchex-s go to the auditor when there are vouchers. But there is not a voucher for a tip. When they give a pullman porter a tip they do not take a voucher for it?
No, but an officer of the department certifies that it is correct and the Auditor accepts that without knowing whether it is correct or not.
What are you going to do about it?
The minister says that there is a voucher for every expenditure. Now he has to admit that there are no vouchers for a great many expenditures.

The hon. member said that if we withdrew one clause of a certain Bill he would allow the estimates to go through in two minutes. Now he will not stand by that and he tries to make out that I made a statement that I will not stand by.

The minister has attributed to me a statement that I never made.
I did not say that the hon. gentleman should withdraw one clause of the Bill, but I said two clauses.
When in doubt take the customs.

Well, I might say tr>
the hon. minister that I have been advised by the Department of Trade and Commerce, whenever in doubt, to take then returns.
Sir Richard Cartwright when he was in this House and when he was in doubt quoted from the Year Book, which was different from the report of the Minister of Customs.

Could we not have one system of returns upon which we could absolutely rely instead of having two systems of returns upon practically the same
matters which returns are not exactly the same?

They are all based upon the customs. The others are compiled from the customs reports. The basis of the whole is the entries of the Department of Customs and we are in a position to have them correct. The Department of Trade and Commerce, I think, arrange the figures in a different way, perhaps using a different table, but their figures are taken from our reports. As to the Year Book, I think it deals with more than mere statistics, but whatever statistics it has appertaining to the trade and commerce of the country must come from us. We are in a position to get the actual facts, no other department is, and we have the statistical staff here in order to compile the statistics and get out a monthly report. At the end of August we can give you the trade for July. We have, I think, the most accurate and up to date statistics of any nation in the world.
The reports of the Trade and Commerce Department are not of much use as far as I can gather from the minister.
I would not say that, but we must be right.
Are the sub-collectors in Manitoba paid by salary or commission or both?
By salary in most of the cases, but in some cases where we have postmasters with power to collect on postal packages they are paid by commission.
Has the minister received any complaints as to the methods pursued by these sub-collectors in Manitoba in dealing with the public?

Occasionally there are complaints, but they are not due to the fault of the officers. In some cases we attend to them. Some of our friends from oither countries, especially from the old country where they are not accustomed to customs troubles, do not know how to make the entry for articles which come out to them, a broker does it for them and then there is a broker's fee charged on the bill and they want to know how it Is that the duty is so much and the fee is so much more. We have to write and find out the facts.
Is it absolutely necessary to have a broker?

With the view of doing away with this annoyance we have instructed our collectors to make out entries if the parties themselves do not know how to make them out for settlers effects. We do not allow the officers to make entries out for the public. That is our rule, and we think it is a safe one. In the case of

settlers' effects we allow the officers to make out the entries when the settlers do not know how to make them out themselves.

I have been informed that a sub-collector has asked a citizen to allow his name to be used as an agent and then the fee would be retained if not directly by the sub-collector, through another member of his family. I do not say this pccurs now, but I am informed by a gentleman who allowed his name to be util-' ized for that purpose that it has occurred. I wish to state to the minister that with regard to the sub-collector at Neepawa there has been a great deal of dissatisfaction not only among the old country people, but among our own Canadian citizens. I do not know whether the Minister of Customs agrees with the ex-Minister of Railways that education is a disadvantage in the Civil Service, but the education of some of these officials, in civility, will stand a good deal of improvement. This particular subcollector has been to my own knowledge very arrogant in his dealings with the public ; if not to the people in his own town, certainly with the outside public. There has been a great deal of delay in customs mail coming through the post office, and I am told people have received invoices three or four weeks before the material would get to the post office. The postmaster has told me that the reason is that the sub-collector will retain in his office the dutiable mail until he has sufficient gathered to fill a mail bag. This is a great hardship to many people who want their goods immediately. Ladies and gentlemen have made complaints to me with regard to this. In some instances the correspondence has been replied to in anything but a civil manner by the sub-collector, and in many instances he has not repdied to the correspondence at all. When I was home at Easter I was particularly asked to bring this matter to the attention of the minister. The complaint does not come from one or two sore heads but is universal. I do not know that I have ever heard an officer so complained of as this officer at Neepawa is in regard to his dealings with the public. The complainants cannot be all wrong and the officer right. I will give one illustration : A Canadian boy graduated in medicine, went to New York, took with him an overcoat of splendid material and in good repair, which was an heirloom in the family ; he put in a year or two in the New York hospitals and he returned to enter into partnership with me in Manitoba. When he was leaving New York he left his overcoat behind aud sent for it afterwards. It came to Neepawa through the customs and he was informed that a certain amount of duty would be levied on it. He explained it was Canadian made, that it had been in the family

for years, that he had not room in his trunk for it when he was leaving New York, but the sub-collector at Neepawa said he would have to pay so much duty. Again the sub-collector was written to but he insisted in holding up the article for quite a large amount of duty. I brought the matter to the attention of the minister and he overruled the sub-collector, as he has in several instances which I have brought to his notice. I do not think any officer who is intelligent would make such a mistake as this sub-collector made, and it is only one of many instances of that sort. If the minister reads a curtain lecture to this gentleman it will, I believe, make him more civil in his dealings with the public. The complaints against him are loud and numerous.

We are all servants of the public and the department strives in every way to impress on the officers the necessity for civility and courtesy even though sometimes their temper may be pretty well tried by some peculiar peopie they occasionally have to deal with. Let me tell my hon. friend that under the circumstances he has mentioned the sub-collector at Neepawa was not at liberty to do anything else than he did. When the hon. gentleman says we overruled the sub-collector, I wish to point out that we have the power to do so, but we do not give the power to the officer to act on his own discretion. If we allowed officers to take this discretion the door would be left open to serious abuses, as the hon. gentleman will see on reflection. These cases have been reported to us, and if we satisfy ourselves as to the correctness of the representations made we act accordingly. We don't want any delay in the customs service or any want of courtesy on the part of the officers, and we will have this matter looked into.
A declaration was ready to be submitted to the subcollector. that the overcoat was Canadian made and he should not have held it up to duty.

I would like to have some of these rules relaxed, but if my hon friend were administering the customs he would see the danger of any relaxation. When the first tariff was introduced, I persuaded the Minister of Finance to put in a provision that any article less than 50 cents in value should come in free of duty and this would save us a great deal of trouble, but my predecessor in the office, Mr. Clarke Wallace, denounced that provision and pointed out that a man in Ottawa could simply write to Ogdensburg and order 50 cents worth of cigarettes every morning and thus evade the payment of duty. We saw the danger of opening the door in that way, because we saw abuses would follow, gome of these regulations may ap-
pear absurd and vexatious, but they are necessary and cannot be relaxed.

Ij. BOKDEN. I wish to ask something further about the system of inspection. In the report of the Civil Service Commission one of the commissioners referred to the tendency in the English outside service to give smaller salaries and higuer travelling expenses so as to induce the inspectors to keep out constantly on the road and I quote from the evidence on that point :
Q. In the English outside service the tendency rather is to give smaller salaries and higher travelling expenses so as to induce the inspectors to go out constantly on the road?- A. The inspectors are expected to make an examination once a year of each port in their district. That you see it requires them to make an inspection and to be around a good deal.
Q. Take Mr. Bremner, for instance, he would not have any inducement to go to Barrington, or an outside outport, in Nova Scotia in the middle of the winter ?-A. Not in the mididle of the winter. He would select his seasons for the difficult points.
Q. And the consequence is that by selecting his seasons for the difficult points the collectors would know almost to a certainty when the inspectors would come around ?-A. I think
so.
Q. If the collectors knew when the inspector is coming around they can always, if there is anything suspicious, cover up their tracks?- A. It would give them a better opportunity but it is difficult for them to cover up their tracks under the system we have in operation.
Q. What are the inspectors' duties. When Mr. Bremner goes to Weymouth, for example, what does he do?-A. The first thing is to count the cash. He then looks over the work of the port, and compares the entries with the manifest. The manifests are not filed in the department, they remain at the port as a record of the goods coming in.
By Mr. Fyshe:
Q. The manifests are kept at the port?-A. Kept at the port. That is the manifest of goods received.
Q. What check has the department at Ottawa that the full duties are being received? -A. We have the entries. The entries are sent to Ottawa when they are passed by the importer.
Q. And these correspond with the manifest? -A. They are supposed to, and the inspector checks them to see that they do.
Q. Would the inspector go .over all the manifests that have accumulated since the last inspection?-A. At small ports he would, hut not at large ports, it would he impracticable.
Q. You say that in most cases the collector would know that the inspector was coming around?-A. I think he would.
Q. The inspector would surely not notify him ?-A. No.
Q. Why should he know then?-A. He may know that he is at a neighbouring port, and that he will likely take the ports in their turn.
Q. Under the system of bank inspection the inspector drops down when he is utterly unexpected, and when there are two or three branches together he does not take them ail at once, hut goes away and returns again?- A. At the large ports there is a system of check that tends to prevent any fraud by the officers. The danger is at the small ports where there is only one officer. At the other ports one officer is a check upon the other.
Then there are some illustrations given of the results at small ports. For example, there is some evidence given with regard to the defalcation at Drummondville :
Q. How long did that defalcation go on?- A. I suppose some months.
Q. That office was inspected, I presume ?-A. Yes.
Q. Did the inspector discover the defalcation ?-A. Not at first, for the reason that the manifest was destroyed. It was a manifest from Montreal and he took the last number for the year.
Further on:
Q. It is strange that one of the questions asked by the commission in 1892 was what was to hinder a collector at a small port from suppressing an invoice and putting it into the fire ? That is really wihat happened at Drummondville?-A. He suppressed the last manifest of the series for the year. I think that can be checked, hut our work of late has been so hard that it is difficult to keep pace with it.
Then there is a large amount of evidence, which I will not quote, with respect to some frauds practised in Montreal by a man of the name of Hobbs. It seems that he was enabled, by a certain system which he invented, to entirely circumvent the inspector, Mr. Meunier, who was suspended, and the collector at Montreal says he has been under suspension ever since. It would seem to me, from these and a number of other quotations which I might make from the evidence, but with which I will not weary the committee, that something might be done to increase the efficiency of the system of inspection. So far as I am concerned, I would be glad to support the minister even in increasing the staff if it were necessary to make a thorough and effective inspection of every port at least once a year. It does strike me, from what the minister himself has stated, that two inspectors for the entire province of Quebec would be regarded by any large Institution of the country as entirely inadequate for the purpose which they are supposed to serve. There must be a very large number of ports iu the province of Quebec, and I suppose a much larger business is done at Montreal than at any other port in Canada. I would think that the attention of the department might be very well directed not only to tlie system of Inspection, but possibly to the putting into practice of some better system of check than seems to be in vogue at the present time. The inspection to which we had reference the other even-

ing at the port of Huntington in British Columbia seems to have been singularly inefficient on two occasions. On the first occasion, shortly before the defalcation was discovered an inspection took place, which did not result in ascertaining that the public moneys were being misappropriated. Then, the inspection which did result in discovering the defalcation was not a very effective one, as the minister very candidly acknowledged, because it was not discovered at that time that some $6,000 additional had been misappropriated, and that remained undiscovered for three or four years. Has the minister taken the suggestions in the evidence in this regard into consideration?

I cannot say that I have in the sense of utilizing them. The report of the commissioners, so far as the customs is concerned, helps us very little. I do not say that in disparagement of the commissioners, but in commendation of my officers, who have introduced such checks and safeguards as to leave very little that is valuable to us in the suggestions of the commission. There is that difficulty of one officer alone at a port. At a large port like Montreal, if we made as thorough an inspection there through our inspectors as we make at the smaller ports, it would never be finished, if he worked at it all the time. With 178,000 entries in nine months, and with all the way-bills and transfers and manifests and the checking of the cash, it would be impossible. We have to depend largely upon the checks which the officers have upon one another in the office. In Montreal, while the inspector is there a good deal, and watches how things go on from day to day, we have a very thorough collector there besides. With reference to the defalcation mentioned by the commissioners our officer neglected his plain instructions, or it could not have happened. That is not settled yet.
Mr White, in dealing with that, says: 'If the cashier had obeyed orders, a portion at least of the defalcation 'would not have happened.'

The instruction was that when a cheque was handed in for a larger amount than the duty came to, the refund was to be made by cheque. The officer in question knew that, and it was his duty to have returned the money by cheque; but he returned it iu cash. We have now instituted a check which will make it perfectly safe so that this could not happen again. But, as Mr. White says even the banks, with much smaller staffs than we have, and with managers and directors sharp business men, are defeated from time to time.
I think he says something more to the point than that-that
you cannot by any possible system guard against flagrant dishonesty.

The hon. leader of the opposition alluded to the fact that he had information that instead of $4,200 that we got as the result of the first examination, it was $5,800. Inspector Busby is here now, and I inquired about that. It appears that when Mr. Olute made the first examination, he found entries that had not been made, the duties of which amounted to $800. He had the collector have those entries made, and the duties paid by the parties for whom they were made. The goods had gone out of his possession but the entries were there and he made him get the entries from the merchants and get the duty from them. The $800 collected went to the credit of the Receiver General in the usual way, being sent to New Westminster, but Mr. Olute in his report to us did not mention that the $800 was here in that way and so that would be $800 more than the amount mentioned.
What was the customs revenue for the last month and how does1 it compare with the same month of last year ?

It has fallen off. In round numbers, for the two months of the present financial year, the customs revenue is two millions and nearly three-quarters less than for the corresponding two months of last year.
A falling off in any particular line ?
No, it seems to be general and at all the ports. Winnipeg and perhaps Vancouver are keeping up, but in Montreal, Toronto and all the others there is a falling off.
Has the hon. gentleman decreased his staff ? When the revenue increases he increases his staff ?
I do not think we can do that, we have been working the men too hard.
What particular experience had Mr. Charles McNellen, assistant appraiser at Halifax, which resulted in his appointment.
He passed the required examination.
Was he engaged in any particular line of buisness which qualified him for that particular line of business?
I do not remember, he has been in the customs for some years.

There has been some criticism of the fact that he was appointed over the heads of a great many capable officers receiving only $700 or $800 after many years' service, and has now a,

salary of $1,000. The information which comes to me is that he had no particular qualification except that he had some pretty strong political backing.
He has qualifications we believe or he would not be there.
I would like to know what they are.

We try to make these appointments by merit. But, as I said, if a man is recommended to me as being capable and worthy for a position, I have never considered the fact of his being a Liberal a barrier to his appointment.
I am not suggesting that it should be, but I am suggesting that it should not be the sole consideration.

He has been on since 1901.
Mr. R, L. BORDEN. I took the Civ'i'l! Service List of 1907.
He has been permanent since 1904, but he was in the service before that.
I am afraid he has no qualification beyond what I mention.

Do you know him ?
. Mr. R. L. BORDEN. I have heard a good deal about him but I do not know him personally.
As not being able to discharge his duties or what ?

I cannot say I have heard anything more about it than what I have stated. I have a memorandum Ion the subject from a responsible person in which reference is made to other officers in the department who have been there a long time, some of them for ten, or fifteen years or twenty years and who would be fully as capable, if not more capable, than the gentleman who has received the appointment. The statement is also made that he is pretty closely connected to a prominent gentleman in public life, and that circumstance is supposed to account for the passing over of officers of long service in favour of this gentleman. One would hardly imagine the Minister of Cuistoms would be influenced by any considerations of that kind, and thus it is only fair to give him an opportunity of explaining the matter.

The Minister of Customs is human. From what I understand he discharges his duty well. As to the parsing over of those older in the service, it is difficult in handling a large body oif men to avoid matters of this kind. You cannot get any man to think .that his services are not as valuable as those of another man. In a mercantile lioulse the head of the firm has to determine such matters. You canriot follow the rule but promotions must go by length of service. In public life the same conditions must prevail. Other things being equal, I like to see promotion of the men longest in the service. The hon. member (Mr. R. L. Borden) I think perhaps knows as much as I do about this man and with the general confidence he has in me he will recognize that there must be reasons why this is right.

I think it would perhaps be a fair statement to say that I know more about him than the hon. gentleman is disposed to admit. The minister has not given uls many proofs as to this gentleman's special aptitude. There are many officers at Halifax who were worthy of promotion. I do not think that the circumstances of this case as detailed to me are such as to increase the discipline or the honesty of the men in the (service.

Do you not think he has special aptitude for his duties now' ?
, Mr. R. L. BORDEN. I am informed that there are many officers in the service who have displayed more aptitude than this gentleman has displayed.
My impression is that he discharges his duties very well.

As the minister is probably aware there has been and still is great dissatisfaction in Montreal, especially^ among importers in the dry goods trade, dissatisfaction which has been expressed on more than one occasion, regarding the settlement of customs frauds by compromise. There has been even more of that in the last two or three months than previously. It is a matter that while doubtless familiar to the minister is well well worth the attention of the House for a few minutes, and I think we should have from the minister a statement of the policy o<f the department in cases where fraud has actually occurred in connection with the importation of goods. Where a man or a firm is caught in the act of committing a fraud, I understand the regular method is to charge double duty and a fine. If the law' was enforced w'hen cases of this kind were discovered, the importing public would know where they stood in connection with the custom service of the country. The ordinary importer who tries to do his duty by his fellow men, who is careful about his importations and invoicing and costs, who may once in a long time happen to have a bale of goods inadvertently placed in another bale of goods and so falsely or incorrectly entered, such a merchant is generally fined the whole penalty that attaches to the otfence. But where, as in this ease, there is a deliberate falsification that goes on for a period of years and involves a very large sum, it almost always results in a private settlement in w'hich the full penalty of

-.the truth of which contention is seen in the fact that the matter has since been compromised by the payment of a sum of $32,000.
The contention of these manufacturers at the time was that they thought they had a right to invoice goods at cost price. This, of course, is the usual excuse set up by parties charged with infringement of the Customs Act. Had such a contention any foundation in law, and were those setting it up honest men, they would defend themselves before a court of justice rather than be branded as smugglers or attempted smugglers. These compromises are a gross injustice to wholesale importers who respect the law, for the latter are thereby compelled to compete at a disadvantage with those wiho, by defrauding the revenue, can undersell them. But the worst feature is that the government is virtually supporting and encouraging the violators of the law to continue their operations, inasmuch as the fines collected are considerably less in amount than would be the full duty imposed. At the time that the charges against the Zurich silk manufacturers were being investigated, an influential delegation of merchants from Montreal and Toronto waited upon Hon. Mr. Paterson, Minister of Customs, to protest against any compromise being made in the event of the charges being sustained. The promise was given them, at the time, that these representations and protests should have the fullest consideration. Now the charges have been fully proved and a compromise entered into which showed the amount of consideration given by the minister to the representations and pro-tests referred to. This can only be characterized as intolerable injustice, and as such cannot be -too strongly denounced. The gpvernment should not overlook the fact, as they have hitherto done, that the honest, law-abiding merchants of the Dominion are entitled to more consideration than those who treat it with contempt. Thes fines are not contribu-

tions to the revenue. They do not replace the duties of which the government has been defrauded, but are disposed of in some other manner. Now, we ask, how are they disposed of, -and who gets the benefit of them?-for, unless some one gets the benefit, directly or indirectly, it seems to us that there would be less disposition to entertain or make proposals for a compromise of any bind. We may mention in this connection that the customs authorities are now engaged in conducting investigations in two important charges of undervaluation, in other words, of customs infraction. In the event of the charges being sustained, are we to expect the continued adherence to the disgraceful system of compromise which has become so frequent and so odious? The fullest penalty provided by the law should he imposed, and with it a wide publication of the fact. The new council of the Montreal Board of Trade have an excellent opportunity to benefit the mercantile community by faking up the question with a determination to put themselves on record and to impress upon the government that what the merchants ask for is not by any means a favour, but in every respect one of right and simple justice.
That was followed, a week later, by another editorial, still more explicit. The following is from the 1 Shareholder ' of Montreal, March 20, 1908:
Customs frauds.
In last week's issue of the ' Shareholder ' reference was made to the settlement, by the Customs Department, of charges of defrauding the revenue made against a number of Zurich silk manufacturers. The settlement refered to consisted of releasing the seized imports on the manufacturers paying to the government a sum of $36.000

Evidently the figures were a little higher than at first stated.
-which were far from being equal to the amount which the customs law calls for under such conditions. The law distinctly lays down the penalties to be enforced against those infringing it, and when condemnation takes place there should be no hesitation in punishing the guilty parties. Compromises have been entered into again and again, and offenders have been dealt leniently with, on the ground that to enforce the full penalty would drive them out of business. This is misplaced sympathy, for such men should never have been in business. Any sympathy should be extended to the honest importers who comply with the law and have to compete with their dishonest competitors. The merchants deprecate in the strongest possible manner any compromise under such circumstances, contending that such is a gross injustice to them. They have again and again sent deputations to Ottawa to protest against them, but this without avail. What course they should now adopt is under consideration, and we would suggest that the matter should he brought up in the House of Commons, under the guise of a motion for the production of all documents relating to every violation of the Customs Act.
Were this done, the public would be greatly surprised at the information thev would receive. At the present time the Customs Department has under consideration two very serious charges. One of these is against John B. Ellison & Sons, wholesale woollen importers of this city, with headquarters at Philadelphia. The other is against Jacob Rohner, of Rebstein, Switzerland, manufacturer of Swiss embroideries. The commercial standing of these two houses, which have been doing a large business in this country for a number of years, is such that it is highly essential that the public should know whether the charges are true. If they are untrue they should be relieved from the stigma which the charges involve^ and that release should be publicly proclaimed. In these two cases, as is frequently done, the goods were seized and were only released when the deposit called for by the customs authorities was put up. This being done, it becomes the duty of the customs authorities to file an information before our courts, and thus afford the accused an opportunity to defend themselves and establish their innocence. In that case, should failure on the part of the incriminated to set aside the grounds of complaint result, the commercial community would be put in possession of the actual facts. In giving, as we have done, the names of those who are charged, as above stated, we are actuated solely by the desire to avert from others the suspicions that might attach to them, and also to afford the accused occasion to take the community into their confidence and relieve them of the stigma which a seizure for infraction of the revenue involves. In conclusion, we may say that we will gladly open our columns to any who desire to enter into explanations relating to the action of the customs authorities.
These editorials make it apparent that there has existed a feeling of dissatisfaction on the part of the importing trade of the city of Montreal. The dry goods association, especially, through their president and secretary, have repeatedly put themselves on record with the department protesting against these compromises which are made in secret, and which hang firms up, as it were, between heaven and earth, where they are not guilty or innocent, but whose cases are, in the language of the Scotch verdict, not proven. It is felt that a firm which gets into trouble with the customs officials have a right to vindication or they should be punished. When a seizure has been made without proper evidence and the firm is not guilty of what it is charged with, that (firm is entitled to the fullest vindication and it is entitled to have every business man know that the charge was not sustained. If, on the other hand, it has been found guilty of a serious infraction of the customs law which has been going on year after year and by which it had profited to the disadvantage of its competitors it ought to be pnuished and punished severely, and these facts ought all to be absolutely apparent. But, to have it compromised, nobody knowing whether the firm was guilty or innocent, is neither fair to the firm nor to_ the community as a whole. Honest importers,

men who are careful not to engage in anything of this kind, are fully entitled to protection. When a business firm is most scrupulous in all its dealings with the customs, it is a very serious thing for that firm to be undersold by other firms which are less scrupulous, and nineteen-twentieths or our trade being strictly honest, the competition of the twentieth-twentieth which reduces the price is unfair and unjust. I would like to ask the minister to give us a statement of the policy of the government in this respect, to tell us whether there has been a reform and an improvement in this system or whether the system of compromise is going on just the same. We would like also to know what are the actual facts with respect to these Zurich silk manufacturers, John B. Ellison & Sons and Jacob Rohner, of Rebstein, Switzerland. What has been done, what was the offence, have they been convicted or acquitted ? If they have been convicted, what has been the extent of the punishment ? What were the extenuating circumstances, if any ?	1 think there can be
no doubt that the sentiment is pretty generally spread abroad that there is a lack of severity in the punishments inflicted which will simply lead to a repetition of these offences on the part of the less scrupulous portion of the business community. I can assure the minister that the matter has been, to the merchants of Montreal, a source of very great dissatisfaction, and they would, I think, read with considerable interest what the minister might say in reply to what has been said to-night.

You have opened up rather a large question, and one which I have already dealt with. The seizing officer would make an investigation. We do not want to do any injury to any one, and if a sufficient amount is deposited to the credit of the receiver general, the party against whom a seizure has been made is allowed to conduct his business. The case is reported to Ottawa and then it goes through the process I have already described. The party is allowed thirty days to put in his defence. The evidence is then gone into by an examining officer who is generally, although not always, a lawyer. Mr. McLean, who .died the other day, discharged this duty. The evidence is gone over and set forth in fis plain and concise a manner as may be for the commissioner to peruse. Tie looks over the report and if he approves of the report which has been made by the officer he sends his recommendation based upon that report to myself where it is finally dealt with. Under a clause of the Act the head of the department may confirm or vary the recommendations or he may refer it to the courts. You will have to trust in a large measure to Mr. AMES.
the department in administering this matter, to have confidence in them or have no confidence in them. The disclosure of the names of the parties from whom seizures had been made might result in injustice to a great many men. Some parties have called for stringent measures in dealing with these cases, but when I have had interviews with them and when I have asked them if they thought it desirable that we should make public every seizure and the name of the firm from whom the seizure was made and the decision given, I understood them to say that they did not propose that. I agreed with them because a grievous wrong might be done. A merchant in Montreal or Toronto, or some other place, in whose integrity I would have as much confidence as I have in iuv own, might perhaps have a shipment of goods and in that shipment, coming from a packer, perhaps there might be a small parcel purchased at another place and sent forward to the packer to pack it in the case. It has come out to this country without it being noted on the invoice that there is a package included in the case. The person sending the case does not mention that that parcel has been sent. It comes to the custom -house, one package in ten is selected at random and goes to the examining warehouse. The other nine do not. It happens that the very case in which the inclosure is goes to the examinin-ing warehouse. The examiner opens it, there is the parcel of goods, not appearing on the entry, no invoice filed, no entry made, the goods having come into the country illegally.
In that case you put on the maximum penalty.

No. These gentlemen bring letters from the exporters ex- ' plaining it was their error. My predecessor in office told me that enclosures ought to be forfeited every time because it was only one case in ten that went to the examining warehouse. But where we are satisfied there is no fraud we impose double duty. Now, as to publicity, it might be very unjust and very unfair to a concern to give publicity, and the member for Brantford recognized, when in asking for the seizures and the penalties he forebore to ask for the names. The best houses in this country have been seized and fined for customs infraction, and if that bare fact were to go out without the explanation it would be very injurious to the firm. In many cases the exporters admitted it was their fault and that the importer knew nothing about it. If the House took the responsibility of asking that the name should be divulged, in fairness to these firms it would be necessary to bring down

all the facts of each case. To state the bare fact that a firm was fined without giving the explanation would be very unjust and would involve its reputation and standing or perhaps its fortune. I do not see how the ' Shareholder ' gets hold of these things. Our officers are sworn to secrecy. The hon. gentleman says the party was fined $32,000 with reference to these silks, and if that be so it is a pretty heavy penalty.
The undervaluation had been going on for a number of years and large quantities had been brought in.
It extended over three years. It is a pretty heavy penalty but there was no compromise in that case.
They were not fined the maximum penalty.
No. But we did not compromise. We had three times that amount of cash in hand deposited by that house and we could have forfeited it if we had wanted to.
Was it not a compromise when you had the money in your hand and could take it ?
No. We adjudicated on the case and came to the conclusion that the penalty exacted was sufficient and there is no compromise about it. We did what we considered to be just.
How did you arrive at the amount of the penalty ?

It is a very difficult matter to determine what these silk goods are worth. I believe one of our appraisers estimated that some of these goods were as much as 30 per cent under value but we have to ascertain the cost of these goods in the country whence they are exported and that is a very difficult matter to determine. We had deputations from Montreal and Toronto about this and one gentleman from Toronto was very severe and wanted the last pound of flesh. Now, we sent samples to this gentleman who had first class knowledge of the business and we asked him to put a valuation on these different lines of silk. The fact is that in some of the lines we sent up he put a value lower than the man entered the silk for. and on which the seizure was made. That will show you the difficulty of valuation in such a case. I understand that the undervaluation ran from 6 per cent to 25 per cent.
What is the total for the three years ?

I cannot say. The case is not settled yet. This firm wants its
deposit back and they are going to the courts to try and get it back.
Would it not be better to allow all these cases to go to the courts and have a judicial decision between the government and the merchant. Then there would be no charge of favoritism.
Every case can go to the court on appeal from our judgment.

The ,fact that few go shows that they are let off lightly.
Mr. PATERSON'. Not at all. Very severe penalties are provided by the law and the Customs Act is very severe and often people will not go to the courts even though they feel they are wronged. They practically have to bring their whole business into court and great delay and loss would be entailed by that procedure. We had a Montreal case which I did not want to deal with and we sent it to the courts and it took weeks to dispose of it. I would be glad if we could send every one of these cases to the courts, but I suppose it would take twenty years in the courts to do the work we do in the department in one year. It may be said that we do it in a rough and ready way, but I believe equity and justice are served. In one case which went to the courts where there was undervaluation charged, the judge heard the whole ease and he hesitated greatly at my putting on the full penalty. This might occur by parties making consignments to themselves at the wholesale price ; but a year or two ago we made the law very explicit. We said that where parties consign to themselves, not having made a sale prior to receiving the goods, they may come in, not at the cost price, but at the wholesale price; but if through an agent they have sold these goods to different customers throughout the country, and then bring the goods in at the wholesale price, that is a violation of the law, because where the goods have been sold prior to their being received on consignment, we require the value for duty to be the value at which the goods were sold.
Is it not a fact that this species of crime is on the increase owing to the leniency of the department in dealing with it ?
No. If the hon. gentlemen were administering the law, he would think that we were anything but lenient. We have very few repetitions by the same house.

I quite agree with the minister in making a distinction between an involuntary infraction of the law through ignorance and a deliberate attempt year after year to defx-aud the customs. In the

first case, it would be in order for the minimum penalty to be imposed; but in the second case, I do not think the government are justified in compromising. It seems to me that it would be better to allow the matter to go to the courts and have such a penalty imposed as would deter others from doing the same thing.

If we thought there was a deliberate attempt to defraud the revenue, especially if it were repeated after a warning, we would not hesitate to take that course. But in many cases the goods have passed our appraisers and have been accepted by us, and the parties plead that fact. They say:	Your officers saw the
goods; they opened and examined them; if the valuation was wrong, why didn't you tell us at the time? If commissions are dutiable, we did not know it; why didn't you tell us? Why did you let us go on year after year? and now your officers come and seize our goods and the man who seizes them gets part of the fine.' I wish I could throw the cases into court: but ten courts could not carry through all the cases and hear all the pros and cons.

Could the hon. minister give us any information regarding the importation of uniforms from England by officers of the militia force ? I understand that practically a prohibitive duty is put on uniforms, but that if a claim is made to the department the duty will be refunded. Has that been settled yet?
That rests wholly with the Minister of Militia. Whatever he does in the matter I have no objection to ; but if the goods come in, they have to pay the duty.

Thirty per cent for British since last year.

I,. BORDEN. I have had some representations on this subject from officers of the militia, who thought it was a little hard and unjust, when they spend a good deal of time and money in qualifying themselves to serve their country, to be obliged to pay a heavy duty on their uniforms. What was the object of the change in the law in that respect?

Up to last year all articles imported by every branch of the government came in free; but all along I have contended that the better plan was to let each department look after iself. I did not think it right that a department of the government should buy goods outside, where there was no duty against them, when the same goods could be got in this country. In other words, the clothing could be bought in England aud brought In free of duty Mr. AMES.
when it might be got from our own manufacturers. Uniforms' come in under that.

He will have to pay the duty and get it out of the Militia Department.
What form has the application to take? Has he to get a certificate from the Customs Department that the duty has been paid, and then make an application to the Department of Militia for a refund?
The Militia Department will either take an extra vote out of which to pay the duty on the uniform and give it back to the officer ; otherwise the officer will have to bear the expense himself.
In spite of this practically prohibitive duty, many officers are in the habit of buying uniforms in England and' paying excessive duties upon them, for the reason that they cannot get them here.
Yes, they can.

Quite as well.
I very much doubt it.

speechtext: He cannot get it back.

I could not say. I would rather the minister answered for himself. Possibly for goods ordered before he may have done something, but he must answer for that. I cannot say.

and got a refund from the Militia Department?
No.

No, I think not.

There is considerable cloth made in Canada at the present time for the tunics. The cloth for the men's tunics is made here.
I am talking about the officers' uniforms.

If the officers look around they can get as well made military clothing in this country as in Great Britain, it can be trimmed as well and made as well. This I think is one of the wisest provisions in the new tariff, doing away with the granting of government work to outside tailors and manufacturers of all kinds. Formerly all classes of machinery and everything required by the government came in competition with our own manufacturers. This item in regard to military uniforms was put in the tariff with all the other departments, they are all placed on the same footing. Our manufacturers are delighted that the government have taken that stand, which is only a reasonable one. You cannot sell a dollar's worth of goods to the United States government that is made outside of their own country, and I would like our government to go further and take that same stand. One of the great troubles we have had in Canada in the past in certain manufacturing industries has been the large purchases made by the government from the United States, England and other places that came in competition with our own products. In regard to uniforms I can tell the officers that they can get as good uniforms and just as cheaply here as anywhere in the world.

I must congratulate my hon. friend on his protectionist principles. I agree that it is an excellent thing to patronize home industries and to have the uniforms made in Canada as much as possible. But I am right in saying that a refund was given from the Militia Department for duty paid to the Customs Department. The minister may recollect my going to him on one occasion with a question that came up in connection with the Lennoxville grammar school. not see how this regulation is helping the manufacturer of uniforms at home.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: There certainly is no general policy of refund. The argument for imposing duty on government importations generally, in addition to what the Minister of Customs has mentioned, is this : It is convenient for comparison in the cases of tenders, ; for example jone party would tender for goods knowing it was the practice to import goods for the government free and would make a lower tender, placing the Canadian manufacturer at a disadvantage. Then there would be disputes. A man would say : I always assumed we would have the goods free. The whole thing was left in an uncertain condition. Difficulties would arise. I do not think the system was abused as much as some gentlemen thought, but it led to abuse, misunderstanding and sometimes inequalities in the matter of competition, so we thought it better to say that any one competing for the sale of goods to the government must quote a duty-paid price.

I suppose the minister, in locating a customs office, considers whether the port is a railroad centre and its distance from the international boundary. I have urged in this House, and have called the minister's attention personally, to the town of Carman, in the constituency I have the honour to represent. It is one of the largest constituencies in Manitoba, and yet there is not a single customs office within its boundaries. Carman is a large town, the centre of three lines of railway-the Canadian Northern, the Jim Hill system, and the Canadian Pacific Railway. The minister knows that the board of trade have repeatedly made requests for the establishment of a port of entry. They have written nice letters-I have read some of them. If he will look at the files, he will see that great difficulty 'has been experienced through want of a customs officer there. I have pressed it forward, however, with all the urgency possible and inquired about it no later than yesterday when I was told that special exertions are being made, that more than one person have been at work on it for some time past and I was informed that possibly it might be ready in the course of a few weeks. I cannot speak more definitely than that, but I am very hopeful it will be possible to present the return before the end of the present session.
